## Reading

**epigraph**
*The plant behind this glass flowers once in its life. Most are harvested first.*

**whoYouAre**
Every time you return to a place you love, you're bracing before you arrive. The café that might have closed. The field that might be houses now. The woods at the end of the lane, with a car park where the gate was. Everyone else sees the view. You're counting what's left.

You start missing things while they're still here. So you touch them as little as you can. You don't pick the flower. The stone stays where it was. The path looks the way you found it. People sometimes take that for strictness, and you'd rather they did. It's easier than saying how much it hurts to watch something thin out while everyone around you is still enjoying it. And easier than admitting the fear under that one: that some day you'll be part of the reason it went. When other people arrive, your care means there's still something there for them to love, whether anyone thanks you or not.

**yours**

1. The agave, the plant tequila is made from, grows for years before it flowers, and it flowers only once. A stalk shoots up from its heart, sometimes twenty centimetres in a day. It makes its nectar at night, and bats come for it and carry the pollen. Then the plant dies. As tequila grew, producers stopped letting their agaves flower. A plant spends the sugar in its heart on that one flower, and once it has flowered it's no use to the still. Stopping the flowers took away a main food of the nectar bats, and their migrations shifted.
2. David Suro-Piñera produces tequila. With a bat scientist, Rodrigo Medellín, he helped start a programme that asks growers to let some of their agaves flower, at least five in every hundred, and to show that bats have fed from them. Letting them bloom, Medellín said, is "considered a waste": a plant that flowers can't be harvested for tequila. One of Suro-Piñera's own tequilas was on the programme's first list. And his reason, in his own words, wasn't only the bats. It was "the necessity of genetic strength": plants left to flower make the crop stronger for later. The lesser long-nosed bat, one of the agave's bats, came off the US endangered list in 2018, the first bat ever taken off because it had recovered. Its recovery had many causes.
3. The bats, I like to think, came back one year to the fields they'd always fed from and found the flowers gone. That's your fear, exactly. What Suro-Piñera asked for is what you already do everywhere you go: leave some of it standing, even when taking it would make perfect sense, so there's something there for whoever comes next. His reason is yours too. You don't hold back only because you're soft about wild things. You hold back because you feel responsible for what a place will be long after you've left it.
4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Martini, the drink with more poems and jokes to its name than almost any other, made with blanco tequila: the clear kind that never sees a barrel, made from agave alone. I'd pour Suro-Piñera's Siembra Azul, though it isn't the bottle on that first list. A delicate, herbal blanc vermouth goes with it. No peel, no garnish, so nothing is laid over the plant's own smell. Then one teaspoon of peach liqueur. When an agave flowers, its sugar goes to the nectar instead of the still, and I like to think that spoon is the sweetness the still never got. I chose fruit rather than a flower. You'd leave the flower where it grows, and a peach is there to be picked. It's served small and very cold, without ice, so it's at its best in the first few minutes. It asks you to pay attention while it's there.
5. You don't have to be the only one watching. The next place you're afraid of losing, don't go alone. Take someone and show them what you see: the thing that's thinning out, the one nobody else has noticed yet. Then there are two of you who'd notice if it went. And I think you'll find that watching it with someone feels less like grieving and more like what it really is: loving it while it's here.

**yours**

Make the caramel syrup ahead. Put 1 tablespoon of water in a small heavy pan and pour 200 g of white sugar on top. Heat it on medium without stirring, just swirling the pan now and then, and watch it the whole time. It goes clear, then pale gold, then deep amber. Take it off the heat at deep amber, as soon as it smells toasted and before any smoke rises: past that point it turns bitter in seconds. Stand back and slowly pour in 200 ml of hot water. It will spit and boil hard, and the caramel will set into lumps. Put the pan back on a low heat and stir until everything has dissolved, then let it bubble gently for a minute or two more, until it's about as thick as runny honey. If you're between two, take the one with more water. 4. In a mixing glass or jar, pour 1½ teaspoons of caramel syrup, 2 dashes of Angostura, then the bourbon (and the water, if you need it). # Pour — In a Minute · The Discoverer (explorer-innocent)

## Cocktail

- **name:** In a Minute
- **tagline:** The smallest things can stop you in your tracks. You let them, they're here for a reason.
- **glassware:** a small stemmed wine glass (about 200 ml), chilled, no ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | white rum, Cuban style (a full-flavoured white rum) | |
| 15 ml | Dolin Blanc vermouth (recommended), or any sweet white (blanc) vermouth | the sweet white style the original was made with |
| 10 ml | rainwater Madeira | a wine that has already had its years |
| 1½ teaspoons (7.5 ml) | orange curaçao | |
| ½ teaspoon (2.5 ml) | grenadine, made from pomegranate | for colour as much as sweetness |
| 1 strip | orange peel | |

**method**
1. Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
2. Before anything else, pour a little of the Madeira into a spoon and taste it on its own.
3. Pour the rum, the vermouth, the Madeira, the curaçao and the grenadine into a mixing glass or a jar.
4. Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 20 seconds, until the outside feels very cold. The melting ice is part of the drink: it adds about two-fifths to what you poured.
5. Empty the serving glass if you filled it, and strain the drink in. No ice.
6. Hold the strip of orange peel over the glass, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink. Then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Try a spoon of the Madeira on its own before it goes in. It took its time getting here.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Someone once put drinks like this in bottles for years, to see what time would do.*

**whoYouAre**
On any walk, you're a few steps behind. Something stopped you: frost that's stayed only in the shadow of a fence, a bee climbing into a flower the wrong way round, a sign you've passed a hundred times and have only now read properly. Somewhere up ahead, someone says "come on". You've been hearing "come on" for as long as you can remember.

You were never dawdling. You wanted to see what it would do. You don't often say how much a small thing can make your day, because it can sound naive, and there's an old, faint guilt about holding everyone up. It isn't being slow that scares you. It's getting busy, and sure, and one day walking straight past something without feeling the tug, and not even missing it. The people who walk with you see more than they would on their own. The ordinary comes back to them new. That's what your slowness gives them, and every so often the thing you stopped for turns out to matter to everyone.

**yours**

1. A Manhattan is usually drunk within minutes of being made. Around 2004, in London, a bartender named Tony Conigliaro started putting some aside instead: Manhattans, and a Cuban classic called the El Presidente, in glass, for years. His question came from wine. Wine changes slowly as it ages, and he wondered whether a mixed drink could be helped by ageing too, if it was done with the same care. For years he tried to interest his customers in the idea. Nobody paid it a bit of attention, he said.
2. In 2009 he opened a bar of his own, a small one on a side street in Islington. That October, a bartender from Portland, Oregon, Jeffrey Morgenthaler, was in town, and was told to ask for the Manhattan that wasn't on the menu. It was five years old. Conigliaro told him the years had brought its flavours together. Morgenthaler, by his own account, thought it tasted like a Manhattan. He went home and tried the idea anyway, in a small wooden barrel, where it takes weeks instead of years. His first batch was gone in a week or two, and before long bars across the world were ageing cocktails in barrels.
3. I like to think Conigliaro gave that bottle its years because he trusted there was something in it, while nobody else was interested yet. That's you. You give an ordinary thing more time than anyone else would, before there's any sign it'll be worth it. And look at what travelled. Not the taste: the man who took the idea home could hardly tell. It was the idea, and the question under it: what happens if you don't hurry? You hand people that question all the time, and some of them take it further than you'd ever have guessed.
4. The cocktail I've made for you is an El Presidente, a Cuban classic that became popular far beyond Havana, and a stirred one: white rum and a sweet white vermouth, with a little orange curaçao and half a spoon of grenadine for its colour. My real change is in the wine. I've swapped part of the vermouth for Madeira, a wine the law won't let anyone sell until it has had years, because Conigliaro's question came from wine. So some of the time he was asking about is in there already. It's stirred cold and served in a little stemmed wine glass, chilled first, with an orange peel twisted over it, and it's ready the moment it's made. You're usually the one giving things time. This once, somebody else did the waiting for you.
5. Busy comes for everyone, and the stopping goes first. You won't hear it go. So have one thing going that can't be hurried: a cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a question you haven't looked up yet. Look in on it now and then. And when someone up ahead says "come on", take the minute. It's usually the best one of the walk.

### Image brief

> A small stemmed wine glass, chilled and faintly frosted, stands on the boards of an old wooden garden table on a clear winter morning, beside a low picket fence. Low sun lies across most of the table, but a thin stripe of white frost has stayed in the fence's shadow, and the glass stands right at its edge. The drink is clear and still, a pale gold with a faint rose blush, no ice, with a strip of orange peel resting inside the glass. Beside it lies a small open field notebook with a pencil sketch of a bee climbing into a flower, a pencil across the page, and a small brass hand lens. The one impossible detail: on the sunlit boards, the glass's own small shadow has kept a crescent of frost, the only frost outside the fence's shadow, as if the glass had stopped for it too. Palette: soft aqua in the sky and in the frost's cool shadows, pale winter gold in the sun, raw weathered wood.

- **Glass and drink:** a small stemmed wine glass, chilled, no ice. Stirred, so **clear, not cloudy**. **Colour:** pale gold with a faint rose blush. That's my estimate from the bottles: a white rum; a blanc vermouth, "perfectly clear" (Codex p. 72); rainwater Madeira, pale to gold by law (Portaria 38/2015, Hester); and half a teaspoon of grenadine, which Wondrich says "adds a healthy color" (*Imbibe!* pdf 217). No page describes the finished drink's colour. Garnish: one strip of orange peel, in the glass. No cherry.
- **Props (story):** the frost stayed in the fence's shadow, and the bee going into the flower the wrong way round, sketched (whoYouAre's own scene: the ordinary thing someone stopped for); the notebook, pencil and hand lens (the persona's imagery: "notebooks and binoculars… small discoveries in nature"; a lens stands for looking closely, at rest).
- **One impossible detail:** the crescent of frost kept in the glass's own shadow. Quiet, and only one.
- **Must not appear:** people or hands (house rule); an apple, an apple tree, Newton, a lightbulb or "eureka" (the persona sheet's half-legend and Wren's trap); a barrel or cask (Morgenthaler's barrel is a coincidence for the dossier, and barrels are the Pioneer's ground); ships, the sea, a harbour, a globe (Madeira's history stays out; this family keeps ships out); lab glassware or charts (the gas chromatography stays in the dossier); a clock, hourglass or calendar (too literal); a cherry; a Manhattan or any second drink; any stored, stoppered or dusty bottle (cut r5: it reads as "leave it", *Overnight*'s ground); readable labels, text, dates or logos; ice in the glass; smoke.
- **Palette:** Pantone 628 C, soft aqua (curiosity and lightness), in the sky and the cool frost shadows; pale winter sunlight; generous empty space around the glass (the persona's imagery line).

# Pour — Why Not? · The Mad Inventor (explorer-jester)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Why Not?
- **tagline:** There's an easier way, but it just isn't as much fun.
- **glassware:** a wide china teacup (about 200 ml), warmed with hot water first
- **contains:** `["gluten"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 11 g | white sugar | about 2½ level teaspoons; use 9 g if your ale tastes sweet |
| 30 ml | water | 2 tablespoons, to loosen the sugar once it's dark |
| 90 ml | malty Belgian-style abbey ale (dubbel style, 6–8%) | low in hops, as Arnold chooses for hot drinks |
| 30 ml | aged rum (40–43%) | colonial taverns heated rum with beer and sugar |
| 5 ml | fresh lemon juice | 1 teaspoon; Arnold uses acid sparingly in hot drinks |
| 3 dashes | orange bitters | |
| 1 | small pinch of fine salt | |
| 1 | strip of orange peel | squeezed over the top, then dropped in |

**method**
1. Fill the teacup with hot water to warm it. Measure everything else and set it beside the stove, because once the sugar is ready the rest goes in quickly.
2. Put the sugar in a small heavy pan over a medium-high heat. Don't stir: swirl the pan now and then as it melts, and let it go dark brown and smell toasty.
3. Take the pan off the heat and pour in the water. It will spit and steam, and the sugar will seize into a lump, so keep your face and hands back. Put the pan on a low heat and stir until the lump has melted again.
4. Pour in the ale while you stir (this goes best with two people, one pouring and one stirring). Warm it until it steams, but don't let it boil.
5. Take the pan off the heat and away from the flame. Stir in the rum, lemon, bitters and salt.
6. Empty the teacup and pour the drink in. Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Get someone to pour the ale in while you stir. Then you both built it.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Taverns heated drinks like this with a red-hot iron. This one burns its sugar instead.*

**whoYouAre**
There's a perfectly good way to do it, and everybody knows it. Then there's your way: three extra steps, a part you made from something at the back of a drawer, and someone in the doorway asking what on earth you're doing. It lit you up the moment you thought of it, and that was reason enough.

Some of it falls over. You laugh first, and loudest. What you don't laugh at is the kind voice that says "you could just buy one". It's said with a smile, as common sense, and it lands harder than any collapse, because it turns the best part of your week into a waste of time. What you'd hate most is a life with nothing left to build. Here's what your long way gives people: the kitchen gets louder when you start, and an ordinary job becomes the most interesting thing in the house. When it works, nobody is more surprised than you, and the surprise is catching.

**yours**

1. In the taverns of colonial America, a hot drink on a cold night was often a flip: ale, rum and sugar, heated by plunging in an iron rod that had sat in the fire until it glowed. The red-hot metal did more than warm the drink. It caramelised the sugar and toasted the grain. Then, as Dave Arnold tells it, eggs came into the flip around the time of the Civil War, boiling water took the iron's place, and something crucial was lost.
2. Arnold, who happens to have written one of the books I mix from, decided to bring the iron back, to taste what had gone missing. A pot would have heated the drink. He tried a soldering copper first, which sometimes made the drink taste, as he put it, like sucking on a penny. Then cast iron, then steel, then hot stones, which worked, though he thought better of serving people drinks with stones in them. In the end he built his own electric pokers, for the New York bar he opened with David Chang in 2012. One writer on the cocktail revival described a kid-like "why not?" in everything he did. And when a poker drink was being made, Arnold wrote, everybody perked up a bit.
3. The pot was never really an option, I like to think. You'd know. There's always a pot: the easy way, right there, that would do the job well enough. And there's the other way, the one that takes trial after trial, and leaves everybody perking up. You take the second one because it's the fun one. What makes me smile is that he was right about the iron. It does something a pot doesn't: it caramelises some of the sugar and toasts the grain, right inside the drink. The long way wasn't only more fun. To his taste, it was better. Not every time. But more often than the people who say "you could just" would like to admit.
4. The cocktail I've made for you is a hot flip, the kind colonial taverns served before the eggs came in, and a popular one: a malty abbey ale and rum, the taverns' own spirit, here an aged one, with a teaspoon of lemon, three dashes of orange bitters and a little salt added. I don't expect you to keep an iron in the fire, and Arnold doesn't assume you will either. His own stand-in for a kitchen, the best he's come up with, starts by burning the sugar dark in a pan, and that part I've kept: it gives a toasty, burnt-sugar taste a plain syrup doesn't have. It's the long way round to sweetening a drink, when you could just pour the syrup, and it's there as a nod to the poker and to everyone who'd rather build it. It comes in a warm, wide teacup, the way he insists, because a tall mug traps the fumes, with a strip of orange zest pinched over it.
5. So when you next hear "you could just…", don't explain. Explaining makes it sound like a defence, and it was never one. Hand them the other end instead: the spanner, the bit that needs holding, the ale to pour. Let them be there when it works. I'd bet they'll want to do the next one with you.

**whoYouAre**
Someone opens a jar, and before anyone has said a word you're standing in a kitchen you haven't been in for years. A smell on a stairwell, the first bite of a plum, and you're somewhere else, completely. You can't always remember what year it was. You can remember exactly what the bread tasted like. And whatever is in front of you now, you're really tasting it.

What you play down is how hard it hits. You say "mm, lovely", because you've seen the eyebrow go up across the table: it's only bread. It's never only bread to you. What frightens you is a life with the senses turned down, on a menu somebody else chose. Or a meal with someone who isn't tasting, which is lonelier than eating alone. And look what you do with good things. You tear off the warm end of the loaf and hand it over. You crush a leaf under someone's nose: "smell this". Years later, the taste that takes them somewhere has you in it. That's a lovely thing to leave in someone's life.

**yours**

1. A man who supplied cider to the London bar where Dick Bradsell worked once brought in three liqueurs: a blackcurrant, a raspberry and a blackberry. It was the blackberry that did it. As soon as he tried it, he said, he was "back in that blackberry patch on the Isle of Wight", the island where he grew up. "It was spot-on, that flavour."
2. He made a drink around it, with gin, lemon and sugar: a British drink, at a time when, as he put it, the scene was totally vodka. He started from a drink he already had, a Singapore Sling he'd made at another club, and cut it down into a short one. The blackberry gave it its fruit, and he gave it a more British name: the Bramble, the wild bush that blackberries grow on. At Fred's, the Soho members' club where he worked, it was popular straight off, and before long it had crossed the Atlantic.
3. Hardly anyone was thinking about blackberry liqueur then, and he went with it. I like to think that, for a second, people at Fred's stood in a blackberry patch on an island they'd never seen, and nobody had to tell them. That's how it is with you. A taste doesn't only please you. It takes you somewhere, and you can't help wanting to take someone along.
4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Bramble, now a modern classic: gin, lemon juice and a little sugar, shaken and poured over crushed ice, then the blackberry liqueur poured slowly over the top, so it runs down through the ice in dark threads, and a fresh blackberry to finish. My change is in that pour. Into the blackberry liqueur I stir balsamic vinegar, no more than half a teaspoon, the dark, sweet Italian kind: a cook's pairing for berries. I like to think the berries he remembered were the ones eaten warm off the bush at the end of summer, soft and almost like wine, so the vinegar is there to make the blackberry taste riper and darker, the way those do. It's the sort of thing that raises an eyebrow. Then people taste it.
5. Find the taste that takes you somewhere, the one you could never quite explain, and give it to someone you love. Cook it, pick it, track it down. Don't tell them the story first. Just hand it over, and then let them tell you where it took them. You've been taking people into your places for years. This time you'll get to go into one of theirs, and you'll know that the person across the table is tasting too.

**whoYouAre**
There's a shelf somewhere in your home that would surprise people. Very old books next to very new ones, and a couple you'd rather nobody picked up. You've gone further than the shelf, too: the silent weekend, the long walk, the course your friends teased you about. Each time you return with one thing, a line or a habit, and you want it to last through an ordinary week.

Nobody sees how often it slips. By Wednesday the inbox has it, and part of you decides the real answer must be somewhere else, so you start looking again. What would scare you is a life that stops asking what it's for. But some of it has been working for years without your noticing. The walk you take before a hard day. The song you play in the car before you go in. You'd never call those a practice, and they've been holding you up the whole time. People feel it, too. You arrive more present than most, and sometimes you hand someone exactly the line they needed, with no lecture attached. That line was worth every retreat.

**yours**

1. In 1973 Gary Regan, a young bartender from a small English seaside town, started a new life in New York, where the customers seemed larger than life and made him nervous. So he began arriving at least an hour before his shift. He ate dinner alone at a table, then sat on, taking in the room, telling himself the night would go well.

2. The customers stopped intimidating him, and they still teased him, which he said was how he liked it. Years later he looked back and called that hour meditating, in effect, though he hadn't known it at the time: "I just knew it worked." The idea of mindfulness for bartenders came to him at workshops, and he gave talks on it, saying plainly that he was no qualified teacher. Writing about it, he told bartenders never to take things too seriously, and said that when he was setting up a bar alone, loud music could be his meditation.

3. I like to think the part of his story that belongs to you isn't the workshops. It's the hour before them, when he had no name for what he was doing. The search mattered, I think: it gave him words for it, and with words he could pass it on. But what he was doing was already there, on a working night like any other, doing its job. I'd guess something in your week does that for you, and you've never given it a name.

4. He wrote a book about the Negroni, a renowned classic. In his best-known book, he printed it with the Campari first, then sweet vermouth and gin, the same measure of each, and one odd instruction: build it in any order. The recipe doesn't say why. I like to think there's a whole outlook in those three words. In the cocktail I've made for you, his instruction stays. I've changed two things, so the gin leads and half the vermouth is dry, which makes it brighter and less sweet. Then one addition: a dried bay leaf, torn in half, out of the kitchen cupboard. I put it in for that hour: something ordinary you already had, doing more than anyone gave it credit for.

5. Keep going away. It's where you find the words. But before you plan the next retreat, look at what already carries you through an ordinary day, the walk, the song, the hour you keep for yourself, and give it its proper name. It counts. You're further along than you think, and I'm glad of it for you.

# Pour — Fine by Me · The Trailblazer (explorer-outlaw)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Fine by Me
- **tagline:** You hear “only if” as a yes with instructions.
- **glassware:** a tall highball glass, packed with ice
- **contains:** `["spice"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 45 ml | Four Roses bourbon (40%), washed with Benton's bacon fat (recommended), or any straight bourbon washed with the fat of a smoky, dry-cured country bacon | you wash it yourself, a whole bottle at a time. It's made with pork fat, so it isn't for anyone who doesn't eat pork |
| 7.5 ml (1½ teaspoons) | maple syrup, dark (Grade B style) | as in Lee's recipe |
| 2 dashes | Angostura bitters | |
| 135 ml | dry sparkling cider, 7% or under, well chilled | |
| 1 | large piece of orange peel | |

**method**
1. **Wash the bourbon (about 6 hours, the same day).** Cook the bacon slowly over low heat until the fat has run clear and the edges are crisp, not burnt: fat from overcooked bacon tastes bad. Measure 3 tablespoons (45 ml) of the melted fat. Stir it into a 750 ml bottle of bourbon in a wide container that can go in the freezer. Cover it and leave it at room temperature for 4 hours, then put it in the freezer for 2 hours. The fat sets into a solid layer on top. Lift it off, then pour the bourbon through a clean cloth or a coffee filter back into its bottle. It keeps in the fridge for up to 2 months.
2. In a tall glass, stir together 45 ml of the washed bourbon, the maple syrup and the bitters until the maple has dissolved.
3. Fill the glass with ice and stir for 3 seconds.
4. Pour in the cold cider and stir once.
5. Twist the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Wash the whole bottle yourself. And when it starts following you around, let it.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*The bourbon in this glass owes a lot to someone's leftover bacon fat, and a joke.*

**whoYouAre**
Somebody once told you, "You can, if you do all of it yourself." They thought that would be the end of it. You said fine, and spent your own evenings on it without a word of complaint, because a hard yes is still a yes. You ask for odd things too, half as a joke, and you're often the only one who comes away with them.

You suspected the "only if" was meant to put you off. You took it anyway, in plain sight, with a grin. What frightens you comes later, when the thing you made becomes the thing you're known for, and everyone expects you to keep making it. But here's what your stubbornness gives people: because you carried it the first time, nobody after you has to. They get the yes for free. That's a generous thing to leave behind.

**yours**

1. Don Lee came to bartending from a job in IT. Eben Freeman, a New York barman, told him about fat-washing: stir a melted fat into a spirit, freeze it, lift the fat away, and the flavour stays behind. You may have heard Lee invented it. It's often told that way, but he didn't.
2. A regular at PDT, the bar where Lee worked, had a lot of bacon fat and no idea what to do with it. Lee asked about it, as a joke at first, then asked for some. When he took the idea to Jim Meehan, who ran the bar, Meehan was wary, and fairly: infusions take staff time. Lee could put it on the menu if he did all the infusions himself. In Meehan's words, "in true Don Lee fashion, he did." Early on, Freeman tried Lee's version and said it was better than his own. It became the bar's best-selling drink, and it set off a whole run of fat-washed drinks, made with nuts, chorizo, even olive oil.
3. Whatever Meehan expected, I like to think Lee heard a yes, and got to work. So would you. The rest of it comes later. Lee is proud of the drink, but it nags at him too: he once said it's the one that will probably follow him around for the rest of his life. Years on, an environmental cocktail group even held it up as a sustainable drink. He granted you could see it that way, but said it certainly wasn't what they'd been thinking. I'd guess you know that feeling, of watching something you started go places you never meant it to.
4. The cocktail I've made for you starts where his did: bourbon washed with bacon fat, the way his recipe is printed, with Benton's bacon from Tennessee and Four Roses bourbon if you can get them, or a smoky dry-cured bacon and any straight bourbon. You make it yourself, so the washing is yours to do: warm the fat, stir it into the bourbon, wait four hours, freeze it for two, lift the fat off and strain. A little maple, Angostura bitters and a twist of orange peel, as in his Old-Fashioned. Then I take it somewhere his recipe doesn't go: a tall glass packed with ice, topped with a crisp, dry sparkling cider, so the apple meets the smoke and the maple. I did that as a nod to everyone who took his idea their own way.
5. So let it follow you. Being known for something isn't a fence around you. It's the mark you meant to leave, even if you'd never say so, and it carries on without you holding it up. Walk on to the next odd thing whenever you like, and be glad, out loud, that you made this one.

# Pour — Far Enough · The Expedition Leader (explorer-ruler)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Far Enough
- **tagline:** People go further with you because they trust you to bring them home.
- **glassware:** a heavy double tumbler, one large clear cube
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | Shackleton blended malt Scotch whisky (40%), recommended, or any Highland blended malt Scotch, 40-43% | a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut |
| 6.25 ml (1¼ teaspoons) | rich plum syrup, made at home from ripe plums | a nod to the preserved plums waiting at the last depot on the way back; fresh plums stand in for them |
| 2 dashes | Angostura bitters | |
| 1 | large piece of orange peel | |

**method**
1. **The plum syrup (about 20 minutes; makes about 220 ml, enough for about 35 drinks).** Stone 100 g of ripe plums and throw the stones away whole; don't crack them. Blend the flesh, skins and all, until smooth. Put it in a small pan with 200 g of white sugar and warm it gently, stirring, just until the sugar has dissolved; don't let it boil. Press it through a fine sieve and let it cool. It keeps in the fridge for about a week; if it ever tastes fizzy, throw it out.
2. Put the plum syrup and the bitters in the tumbler, then the whisky, and stir to mix.
3. Add one large ice cube and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
4. Twist the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Drink to the top you turned round from. It was still the right place to turn.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*They turned round 180 km from the South Pole. This glass is for the way home.*

**whoYouAre**
It was your idea in the first place: the hill, the all-day walk, the trip nobody else would have booked. Then, a couple of hundred metres below the top, the cloud comes down, someone has gone quiet, and you hear yourself say it: "Right. Turning round." The groan. The long way down. In the car park you count heads, and nobody notices you're counting.

You'll go as far as everyone can get back from, and not a step further. You wanted that top more than any of them. You swallow it on the spot, so nobody has to feel they cost you anything, and later, privately, you file the day under "didn't make it". The fear is getting stranded somewhere you led people, with no plan that gets every one of them home. And that's what your turning round gives the people with you: they go further in your company than they'd dare alone, because they know you'll turn round in time. You earn that trust every time you turn.

**yours**

1. You may know the story of Ernest Shackleton's ship, crushed in the ice. Years before it, he walked towards the South Pole with three others, Frank Wild, Eric Marshall and Jameson Adams, hauling sledges onto the high plateau. At New Year 1909, short of food, he wrote that he made himself "consider the lives of those who were with me": go on too far, and they could never get back. He kept going south for days afterwards. On 6 January he admitted, that night, that it had to be their last march south with the sledge. Then a blizzard pinned them in their tent for two days, with the food going. On 9 January they left the sledge, pushed on to about 180 km from the Pole, planted the flag, turned their backs on the Pole, and started home. He wrote that failure was theirs, though they had done their best to avoid it. The Scott Polar Research Institute calls it "the brave decision to turn for home".
2. The way home was hunger and storms, from one store of food to the next. He had told one of his men, Ernest Joyce, to lay out the last big store, and he called it the one ray of hope in front of them. When they reached it there were plums and plum puddings waiting. Then Marshall's illness grew worse. Shackleton left him with Adams and pushed on with Wild to catch the ship, and found the hut empty. When they finally got aboard, he wrote of the load suddenly lifted from his shoulders. That same afternoon he set off again, to bring in the other two. On 4 March the whole expedition was safe on board.
3. I like to think Shackleton had been doing one sum since New Year: how far four people could go and still all get back. He gave the weather and the food as his reason, and both were real. But I think the food was the road home, and he turned while it could still get them all back, with that last store counted in. That's you. You go as far as everyone can get back from, you hold your own wanting until the last possible moment, and then you turn. "But all this was not the Pole," he wrote. "And how sadly I realised that I need not say." You know that sentence. You've just never said it out loud.
4. The cocktail I've made for you is a whisky Old-Fashioned, as great a classic as there is. That classic is built from things that keep: whisky, sugar, bitters and water. I've added one that doesn't. The plums at Shackleton's depot were preserved ones, a boxed luxury; mine are fresh and blended into a rich syrup: a nod to what was waiting at that last store, and to the planning that put it there. I'd pour Shackleton, a blended malt named for him and built on a recreation of the whisky his expedition left under its hut in Antarctica, or any Highland blended malt Scotch. It's built over one big cube in a heavy tumbler, the kind of glass that stands steady wherever you set it down, and orange peel finishes it.
5. So stop keeping that file. Every turn-round in it is a reason people still say yes when you ask them to come. And one of these years, choose a top that's only for you, take people strong enough to get there and back, and go. They'll all come home, the way they always do with you. This time, I hope you stand on it.

# Pour — Show Your Working · The Genius (explorer-sage)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Show Your Working
- **tagline:** You'll follow a question for years, then share every part of the answer.
- **glassware:** a tall Zombie glass, filled with crushed ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 ml | gold Puerto Rican rum | the first of the three rums Berry printed |
| 30 ml | gold Jamaican rum | the second |
| 20 ml | Lemon Hart 151 Demerara rum (75.5%), recommended, or any Demerara (Guyanese) overproof rum of about 70-75% | the third, named in the recipe Berry printed; very strong |
| 27.5 ml | fresh lime juice | |
| 15 ml | fresh grapefruit juice | half of "Don's Mix", written out |
| 7.5 ml | cinnamon syrup, made at home | the other half of "Don's Mix" |
| 17.5 ml | falernum, made at home: a lime and clove syrup with rum in it, as they make it in Barbados, but with no almond, no nutmeg and no ginger | a bought falernum may hold almond or nutmeg, so this one is made where you can see what goes in |
| 1 teaspoon (5 ml) | grenadine, plain, bought | |
| 1 dash | Angostura bitters | |
| 6 drops | Pernod (the anise liqueur, not absinthe) | |
| 1 | mint sprig | |

**method**
1. **The falernum (10 minutes, then a day; makes about 375 ml, enough for about 20 drinks).** With a vegetable peeler, take the green zest off 4 limes, leaving the white pith behind. Put the zest and 12 whole cloves in a clean lidded container with 150 ml of the gold Jamaican rum, and leave it at room temperature for 24 hours. Strain it. In a small pan, warm 200 g of sugar with 100 ml of water, stirring, just until the sugar dissolves, then let it cool. Stir the syrup into the strained rum and pour it into a clean bottle. Write everything that went in on the bottle. It keeps in the fridge for a few months.
2. **The cinnamon syrup (5 minutes, then 30 minutes off the heat).** Warm 200 g of sugar in 200 ml of water with 3 cinnamon sticks, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then let it simmer for 2 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it for 30 minutes, then strain. It keeps in the fridge for about two weeks.
3. Fill the tall glass with crushed ice so it chills while you mix.
4. Put everything except the mint in a shaker. The grapefruit juice and the cinnamon syrup go in separately: together they're "Don's Mix", two parts grapefruit to one of cinnamon.
5. Fill the shaker with ice cubes, close it and shake hard for about 10 seconds.
6. Strain over the crushed ice, and top the glass up with more crushed ice.
7. Slap the mint sprig once between your palms to wake its scent, then stand it in the ice.

**closingLine:** *Write everything that's in the falernum on its bottle. Then ask your oldest question out loud.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Once, if you asked what was in drinks like this, you'd hear: rum and fruit juice.*

**whoYouAre**
Years ago, someone gave you an answer that was perfectly true and told you nothing. You nodded, and kept the question. It has come along ever since, at the back of an ordinary week, and now and then another piece falls into place. Nobody would guess that one of your questions is older than some of your friendships.

You've stopped mentioning it, because people expect a question to be settled or dropped by now. Some take you for a know-it-all. It's nearly the opposite: you can't rest inside something you aren't allowed to understand. What frightens you is being stuck for good with an answer you can't get behind. And once you do understand, you lay all of it out, plainly, so nobody else has to take it on trust. People get the whole answer from you, free, and every year it cost you was worth it.

**yours**

1. In 1979, at twenty-one, Jeff Berry started going to tiki bars on his own. At the Tiki-Ti on Sunset Boulevard he asked the old barman, Ray Buhen: "What's in this drink?" Whatever the drink, Ray gave the same reply: "Rum and fruit juice." Berry heard it in bar after bar. Ray wasn't being difficult: he had once worked for Donn Beach, who created the Zombie at his Hollywood bar, and Beach had told him never to give away the bar's trade secrets, in case rival bars copied them. So by the time Berry started asking, many of the old tiki recipes, the Zombie's among them, had become a mystery.
2. Berry had a day job in films. His off-hours went on the question. He read microfilm in libraries, tracked down retired barmen, and their children when the barmen were gone, and learned to read recipes written in code. In 1998 he put it in print that the Zombie's recipe was still unknown. Getting to the bottom of the Zombie took ten years and three books, he said. He found an early recipe in a self-published cookbook from 1950, and in a former headwaiter's notebook, what he calls the original. And he printed a Zombie with every part named.
3. The answer that kept Berry going, I like to think, wasn't a no. He could have lived with a no. It was "rum and fruit juice": polite, true, and empty. You've been handed that answer too, more than once. A shrug doesn't end a question for you. It starts one. And his narrowed the way yours do, from every drink on the menu down to one: the Zombie, and then he stayed with it for years, beside an ordinary job, until he could write the whole thing down.
4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Zombie, the first famous tiki drink and still one of the great ones. Every part Berry printed is in it, and your recipe names each one. Two of them, grapefruit and cinnamon, travel under one old name, Don's Mix, a classic tiki syrup. Here they go in one at a time. The balance is mine: more of the lime, the grapefruit, the cinnamon and the falernum, so it's brighter and fresher. And I make the falernum myself (a sweet syrup of lime, cloves and rum that goes into many tiki drinks), as a nod to all the years he spent asking what was in things: with a bought bottle, you'd have to take the maker's word for it. It's shaken, then poured into a tall Zombie glass full of crushed ice, and topped with mint. It's a big drink and a strong one, made to be taken slowly.
5. One more thing from Berry's story. On his own, he got "rum and fruit juice". When he went in with Ted Haigh, a loud, sociable fellow historian whom one writer called Berry's opposite, he left with a recipe. "The first Don the Beachcomber recipes I got were because of Ted," Berry said. So take the question you've carried longest, and ask it out loud to the person you know who's least like you, the one who'd ask a stranger anything. Ask before you're sure it's a good question. You may get there years sooner, and on the day it all falls into place, you won't be the only one who's glad.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*The vermouth in this glass is there because hardly anyone stopped after the first.*

**whoYouAre**
The bill nobody can split, the call nobody wants to make, the mistake that was only half theirs: it's landed on someone near you. You don't rush. You weigh it up, quietly, and then you say it: "Put it on me." And they go home lighter. That's the kindness in you, and it counts for more than you'll ever let anyone say.

The other half is harder. Someone does you a small kindness, a lift, a meal, an evening of their time, and it's paid back within the week, with a little extra. Owing anyone, even briefly, feels like weakness to you, like leaving a door open that someone could walk through. So your books are always in credit. Plenty of people owe you something. You've never asked for any of it back.

**yours**

1. In 1919, months before national Prohibition began, a wartime law had already made selling drink illegal. That year, the Greenwich Village Inn in New York, which a man named Barney Gallant ran, was raided, and he was arrested along with half a dozen of his waiters. Barney agreed to plead guilty on one condition: that his waiters were let go.

2. He was sentenced to thirty days in jail, and he served far less. Yes, his name really was Gallant. You could say it was his place to answer for, and maybe it was simply good business. But I like to think it was more than that: that he looked at his waiters, who'd only been carrying the trays, and decided the cost was his.

3. You'd have made the same decision, and you'd have called it only fair. What I've always wondered is how it felt for those waiters, going home owing someone that much. You've stood where Barney stood more times than you can count. You've never let yourself stand where they did.

4. The cocktail I've made for you comes out of the old saloons, where people at the bar drank in rounds, taking turns to pay, and hardly anyone stopped after the first. A strong drink was too much for that, and one answer was to split the whisky half and half with vermouth, a wine flavoured with herbs: that's where the Manhattan, a renowned classic, and its family come from. So I kept the equal split, the way the Manhattan's early recipes often had it: rye and sweet vermouth, poured to the same line twice, with bitters, then let it run long over ice with soda and a twist of lemon. The rye dry, the vermouth dark and bittersweet, all of it cold and bright. I kept the split for what you won't allow yourself: something else carrying half the weight, so everyone can keep going.

5. So when someone does something for you, don't pay it back. No dinner in return, no bigger present, no "I'll get you back for this". Every time you square it straight away, you take something from them: the feeling you get every time you say "put it on me". Let them keep that. And for once, you get to be the one who's let off.

**closing line (Tomás's, spec v1):** *Let someone get this one. Don't get the next.* Read against the reading: it agrees with the position (y5), not the creed; it's bar-sized where y5 is life-sized, so they don't repeat each other; and it answers the name.

# Pour — The Long Answer · The Idealist (hero-creator)

## Cocktail

- **name:** The Long Answer
- **tagline:** What you make gives people the words they were missing.
- **glassware:** a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass (about 400 ml), with one large piece of ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 75 ml (2½ oz) | bourbon (any, 40–46%) | the reader's own choice, where the older recipes say rye |
| 30 ml (1 oz) | fresh lemon juice (about one lemon) | |
| 30 ml (1 oz) | fresh orange juice (half an orange) | the reader said many preferred it to orange bitters |
| 15 ml (½ oz) | pomegranate grenadine, home-made (below) | real pomegranate, which Fougner wrote the reputable French makers used |
| 45 ml (1½ oz) | cold seltzer (soda water) | the reader wrote "plain water or seltzer"; I chose the seltzer |
| 1 sprig | fresh mint, lightly bruised | his "improvement", in place of crème de menthe |
| 2 | orange half-slices | |
| 1 small piece | fresh pineapple (tinned is fine) | |
| 1 | fresh cherry, or a cherry kept in brandy (not a bright-red maraschino-style one) | |
| | *for the grenadine:* 250 g pure pomegranate juice (unsweetened; a bottle is fine) and 250 g sugar | nothing else: no orange, no acids |

**method**
1. Make the grenadine ahead. Put the pomegranate juice and sugar in a jar, close it and shake (or blend) until the sugar has dissolved. Keep it in the fridge.
2. Put one large piece of ice in a large, heavy, round-bowled beer glass.
3. Pour the bourbon, lemon juice, orange juice and grenadine into a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake briefly, about five seconds. That leaves room for the seltzer.
4. Strain it into the glass, over the ice.
5. Top up with the cold seltzer (soda water).
6. Press the mint sprig once between your fingers to wake it up. Tuck it into the glass with the orange half-slices, the pineapple and the cherry, the way the reader wrote it.

**closingLine:** *Mint in last, the way the reader wrote it. Then see who writes back.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*This glass starts from a reader's letter to a New York paper, in 1934.*

**whoYouAre**
When something matters to you and the arguing starts, you're rarely the loudest person there. Often you go quiet. The right words turn up later, on the way home, and you can lose sleep over the ones you didn't say. Losing an argument, you get over. Staying quiet when it really mattered, you don't.

Then you make something: a page, a song, a picture, a menu, a message that took all evening. In that, you say all of it, plainly, and you mean every word. Sometimes you wonder whether making things instead of arguing is just a nicer way of hiding. It isn't. An argument changes one mind, if you're lucky. What you make travels. It gives people the words they were missing, and room to join in without anyone being talked down to. That's your way of standing up for something, and it brings people together.

**yours**

1. In the autumn of 1933, with Prohibition about to end, the *Sun*, a New York newspaper, gave a writer named G. Selmer Fougner a daily series to help its readers find their way around legal wine and spirits. Wine writing then tended to be grand and mystifying, and cocktail writing jokey, even crude. Fougner was neither. He didn't talk down to anyone who liked a cocktail or a beer, and he answered readers' questions patiently, however silly. One wanted to know whether all scotch was really made in Australia.

2. When he had a view, he gave it, gently, usually. In 1936, when the grenadine sold in America was mostly imitation, he wrote that the reputable French makers used real pomegranate. And when he didn't know an answer, he put the question to readers all over the country, many of whom had been there when famous drinks began, and they wrote back. The column ran daily until he died in 1941.

3. This was his way of standing up for something, I like to think: not with a speech, but with a daily column, where nobody was laughed at for asking and anyone who knew better could say so. It's your way too. And look at what came back when he asked. More than one reader wrote to him about a single Boston drink, and one of those letters holds the recipe behind the cocktail I've made for you.

4. It's the Ward Eight, Boston's best-known cocktail, built from that reader's 1934 recipe: bourbon, lemon, grenadine and half an orange, squeezed, which he said many people preferred, over a rather large piece of ice in a heavy, round-bowled glass "of the type generally used for beer". Fresh mint goes in with the orange slices, pineapple and cherry he listed, in place of a mint liqueur. "This is an improvement," the reader wrote. He allowed plain water or seltzer; I chose the seltzer. His letter leaves the sugar to taste, so I left out the spoon, because the orange and the grenadine carry the sweetness. The grenadine is made from real pomegranate, for Fougner's column of 1936. Pomegranate's own aromas include mint, so the reader's improvement and the columnist's point share a scent. It's long, bright and tart, a hazy rosy orange, and strong: the reader called his "highly potent".

5. Somewhere there's a thing you made about what you believe, and never put out: the page, the song, the long message sitting in drafts. It's ready. But sending it is the argument, so it waits. Send it, where anyone can see it. Then ask people what they think, and mean the question. Some of the answers will surprise you, and you'll find you were never standing up for it alone.

**closingLine (Tomás's):** *Mint in last, the way the reader wrote it. Then see who writes back.*

**whoYouAre**
The medal's still round your neck, or the last exam's handed in, or the record you hunted for two years is finally on the shelf. Everyone's pleased for you. And by that evening you're quietly reading up on the next one.

People call it restless. It isn't, quite. What you dread is finished: a comfortable life that asks nothing of you, a map with nothing left on it. Going after something far away and hard to get is how you find out what you're made of, and once you know, you need something new to find out about. And you never return empty-handed. You turn up with things nobody near you could have got, and you make far away look like somewhere people can actually go. Everyone you know lives a bigger life because you went. No prize on your shelf is worth as much.

1. Eric Seed was a student in Austria when he first came across the pine liqueur of the Alps, and he thought it would sell in Colorado's ski towns. One writer calls him perhaps the most mild-mannered person in the cocktail business, soft-spoken among loud characters, and then adds that there was "nothing safe or boring about his business". Seed went back to Austria to find a pine liqueur he could bring over, and returned with Zirbenz, which the Hofer family distillery has made since 1797.

2. He could afford one pallet: sixty cases. None of the big distributors were interested, so a one-man wine business carried it, sold as a drink for after skiing. It struggled, though in some places it did well, and a Denver bartender took it on. Years later Seed said the conifer "is hardly an essential bar ingredient". Back then, with that first bottle behind him, he walked into the best liquor store in Aspen and asked what they'd like to carry. That became his way of working. He asked bartenders on both coasts what he should bring over, and went and found it: one asked for Batavia arrack, a rum-like spirit from Indonesia. For a decade, by one writer's account, a visit from Seed to a cocktail bar was an occasion, and nobody knew what rare bottle he'd pull out of his bag.

3. The pine was never the whole point, I like to think. It took him somewhere, it showed him he could, and then came the question you know well: what now? As I see it, his way out was to stop waiting for something new to find him, and to ask other people what they'd like him to find. That way, the map never runs out. You've had that flat evening more times than you'd admit, and his way out is one you can borrow.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a toddy, the classic warm winter drink, for the end of a cold day. The pine goes in first, Zirbenz or any Alpine stone-pine liqueur, three parts to one of aged rum, a pairing its importer suggests for toddies. Then a teaspoon of allspice dram, the kind of bottle Seed might pull out of that bag. I added it for the find that comes next, so the first prize and the one after share a glass. A little lemon, a touch of brown sugar syrup, hot water, all in a glass mug warmed first, and last, lemon zest twisted above the steam, for its scent. It takes a reddish tint from the pine, and it smells of pine, with spice underneath.

5. So the next evening you arrive and it goes flat, don't go looking for a bigger mountain straight away. Ask a friend what they've stopped hoping to find: the book that's out of print, the song they half remember, the place they always meant to see. Then go and get it. You'll never be short of somewhere to go, and a friend gets the thing they'd given up on. I hope your list stays long.

In the mid-eighties, a legendary New York restaurateur named Joe Baum was opening a new restaurant, Aurora, and he tried out a bartender called Dale DeGroff to run its cocktail bar. DeGroff had spent six years behind a hotel bar in Los Angeles, learning spirits and cocktails on his own; the way one book tells it, so he wouldn't lose a good job he knew was beyond his qualifications. I like to think he couldn't have: he could taste that something was wrong, but the answer had to be DeGroff's, and it stayed his. More than thirty years later, the orange is still in the recipe DeGroff gives for it. You treat the people you learn from as if they're holding the answer and deciding when to let you have it. The answers that make you who you are come from somewhere nobody pointed you, and they're yours for good. 4. The cocktail I've made for you is built on the Bullshot, as DeGroff prints it: vodka shaken with beef broth. # Pour — Hold the Shark · The Storyteller (hero-jester)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Hold the Shark
- **tagline:** Your worst days become everyone's favourite stories.
- **glassware:** double old-fashioned glass (about 350 ml), packed with crushed ice
- **contains:** `["nuts"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | Appleton Estate 12 Year Old Rare Casks Jamaica rum (43%), recommended, or any aged Jamaican rum, the oldest you can find | Vic's seventeen-year Wray & Nephew is long gone. Appleton Estate became part of J. Wray and Nephew, the firm behind Vic's rum, in the early twentieth century. |
| 30 ml | fresh lime juice (about one lime; keep half the shell) | measure it: a big lime's juice pushes the drink too sharp |
| 15 ml | orange curaçao (a dry style, about 40%) | |
| 15 ml | toasted almond orgeat (an almond syrup scented with orange flower water), made at home (method, step 1) | the almonds go in the oven first, like anything a cook wants to taste of more |
| 5 ml (1 teaspoon) | simple syrup (1:1) | Vic wrote "a dash" |
| 1 | big branch of fresh mint, standing up out of the ice | |
| ½ | the squeezed lime shell, dropped in | |

**method**
1. Make the almond syrup a day ahead, or that morning. Spread 150 g blanched almonds on a baking tray and toast them in the oven at 180°C for 8 to 10 minutes, until pale gold and smelling toasted. Let them cool. Blend them with 300 ml cold water for a minute, leave it 30 minutes, then squeeze it all through a clean cloth into a bowl. Weigh the almond milk, pour it into a pan with the same weight of white sugar, and warm it gently, stirring, until the sugar has gone (don't let it boil). Off the heat, stir in ¼ teaspoon orange flower water. Bottle it: about 400 ml, two weeks in the fridge.
2. Make crushed ice: wrap a tray of ice cubes in a clean tea towel and bash it with a rolling pin.
3. Squeeze the lime, measure 30 ml of juice, and keep half the shell.
4. Put the rum, lime, curaçao, almond syrup and sugar syrup in a shaker with a big scoop of the crushed ice. Shake hard for about ten seconds.
5. Pour everything, ice and all, into the glass. Pack more crushed ice on top until it mounds over the rim.
6. Push the half lime shell into the ice, cut side up. Squeeze the mint branch once in your hand so it smells, and stand it up beside the shell.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Its name went round the islands long before its recipe did.*

**whoYouAre**
A flat tyre on the motorway, in the rain, with no signal. By Friday it's the best thing anybody's heard all month: there's a tow-truck driver who sang the whole way, a hailstone the size of a plum, and a lorry that people ask you to do again. All of it happened, more or less. You simply know which version deserves to be the one people keep.

What nobody at the table knows is that the bigger the story, the worse it really was. The forty minutes on the hard shoulder, cold, and sure nobody was coming, never make it in. Told plainly, a bad day might sound like weakness. Worse, it might sound like nothing much, and be forgotten by the weekend. So you tell it larger, until the bad day is the small thing in it. The people listening go home believing their own bad week will pass, and might even be funny one day. That's a real kindness, and it's why they keep asking for another.

**yours**

1. Victor Bergeron lost a leg as a boy. Years later, when people knew him as Trader Vic, the man behind a chain of South Seas restaurants and the Mai Tai most people know, he liked to tell them that a shark had eaten it. As he got famous, plenty believed it. Maybe a shark really did. The odds are against it.

2. The plain version goes like this. He left school, then tried one job after another, selling paint and tyres among other things, and none of them lasted. (Yes, tyres. I didn't make that bit up.) In 1934, in his early thirties, he opened a barbecue shack in Oakland with $800 borrowed from an aunt, and ran it as owner, bartender and cook. One writer says that's where the nickname began, with his habit of trading meals for goods and services. Four years later the shack became Trader Vic's, and by the time he died there were more than twenty, across North America, Europe and Japan.

3. I like to think he knew the shark was the better line at a table. But look at the plain version again: the jobs that didn't last, the borrowed money, a cook paying his way in meals, and a name that grew out of it. None of it needs a shark. It's a terrific story as it stands, and it was his all along. So is your own. The version you tell is a gift, and it does people good. The one you leave out would hold the table just as well.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is his Mai Tai, the renowned classic. I built it on his own account of making it, which he dated to 1944: aged Jamaican rum, fresh lime, almond syrup, orange curaçao, a dash of sugar syrup, all shaken hard with shaved ice, then half the squeezed lime shell and a branch of fresh mint standing up out of the glass. This one keeps close to his formula, and the main change is mine. He used a French almond syrup. I make mine at home and toast the almonds to pale gold first, the way a cook would, as a nod to the cook he was before anyone called him Trader. I like to think the cook in him would have approved. It's golden and cold, sharp with lime first, then round and nutty underneath.

5. So keep telling them. The shark stays: people need it, and you're good at it. But once, tell one exactly as big as it was. I'd bet the table goes just as quiet. And what they'll remember afterwards won't be the shark. It'll be you.

**closing line:** Tomás's, cut to its first sentence in the collection review (2026-10-06, D13 V6): *Take the almonds to gold before anything else: that's where the taste is.* The room's version went on: "Next time someone asks how it went, give them what happened, nothing added." It agrees with y5's position, not the creed. y5 avoids "nothing added" so the two don't repeat each other.

# Pour — Day Job · The Superhero (hero-magician)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Day Job
- **tagline:** You make difficult things look possible, and leave people feeling capable.
- **glassware:** nick-and-nora glass (about 150 ml), chilled
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 ml | white rum, Cuban style (light and dry, unaged or lightly aged), 40% or stronger | the recipe asks for Cuban or Puerto Rican; below 40% the drink goes thin |
| 15 ml | sweet (red) vermouth | |
| 7.5 ml | white crème de cacao | clear as water, and it tastes of chocolate |
| 5 ml (1 teaspoon) | orange curaçao (a dry style, about 40%) | |
| 5 ml (1 teaspoon) | grenadine | |
| 15 ml | fresh lime juice: half a lime, squeezed by hand | measure it: a whole lime makes the drink too sharp and too weak |
| 1 | wide strip of lime peel, cut from the same lime | |

**method**
1. Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes.
2. Before you cut the lime, take one wide strip of peel off it with a vegetable peeler, green only, none of the white underneath. Set it aside.
3. Cut the lime in half. Squeeze one half over a jigger with your fingers, nothing else, until you have 15 ml.
4. Put the rum, vermouth, crème de cacao, curaçao, grenadine and lime juice in a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold.
5. Strain it into the cold glass.
6. Hold the strip of peel over the drink, green side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top. Lay it on the rim.

**closingLine:** *Half the lime, squeezed by hand. When you're next introduced, bring up something the introduction doesn't cover.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Its first maker put out booklets of the bar's drinks. This one's in none of them.*

**whoYouAre**
Most days you're easy to miss: quiet in a meeting, with a joke that lands a second too late. Then something turns up that only you can sort out, like a friend's figures that won't balance the night before they're due, or a letter that has to be exactly right. For an hour you're someone else entirely. Afterwards you go back to being easy to miss, and that part is on purpose. You'd rather nobody near you felt outshone.

Ask which of the two is the costume, and you'd hesitate. Years ago, without quite noticing, you decided the quiet one was the disguise, and the ability was the real you. So you keep it sharp, every day, because going rusty would feel like disappearing. The people you're with get someone who could make them feel small and chooses, every time, to make them feel capable instead. That's worth more to them than the ability.

**yours**

1. Constante Ribalaigua came to Havana from near Barcelona as a child. At sixteen, as he told it later, his father, a bartender himself, asked if he'd like to learn the trade, and he said yes. He made his name at La Florida, the Floridita. In 1935 he bought it, and by the end of that decade he was rich, and known abroad too. He's remembered as quiet and reserved, and not much to look at. And every morning he still put on the white jacket and went behind the bar to mix drinks.

2. He squeezed every lime by hand, with his fingers only, though he was one of the first to put electric mixers on a bar. He told a journalist in 1935 that he made up a new drink every day, "as self discipline". Among the drinks he created was the Floridita: rum, red vermouth, a little chocolate liqueur and lime. He put out booklets of the bar's recipes, and for reasons we don't know, that one isn't in any of them. A visiting bartender, Trader Vic, came across it in 1938, put it on the first menu of his own place, and printed it years later. Without him, it might have been lost.

3. I like to think the jacket was the point: he no longer needed it, and he chose it anyway, morning after morning. I recognise you in that. You'd probably call the ability the real you. I'd call it the jacket: you put it on for other people. Who you are is the one who keeps choosing to. And of everything he made, one of the drinks that lasted is the one that isn't in any of his booklets.

4. The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Floridita, with two changes of my own. It's white rum, red vermouth, a little crème de cacao (a chocolate liqueur as clear as water), and grenadine and orange curaçao, one spoonful of each, shaken hard and strained into a slim stemmed glass that's been in the freezer. My first change is half a lime instead of a whole one, because a whole one makes it too sharp. Squeeze it with your fingers, the way he squeezed his limes. The second change is the twist: the lime's own peel instead of orange, so the lime that balances the drink scents it too. You'd only notice it if you knew, and that felt like you. It tastes of chocolate and lime, and it's a delicious one.

5. People will keep introducing you by what you can do: "this is the one who can sort anything out." When it happens again, let them, and then add something about you that has nothing to do with it: the song you can't stop playing, the town you'd move to tomorrow, something you're hopeless at. Watch which one they ask about. And let the quiet one be introduced too. It was never the disguise.

**closing line:** Tomás's: *Half the lime, squeezed by hand. When you're next introduced, bring up something the introduction doesn't cover.* It agrees with y5's position and borrows none of y5's words (R4).

# Pour — No Promises · The Lovable Rogue (hero-outlaw)

## Cocktail

- **name:** No Promises
- **tagline:** You never said you'd come. You always do.
- **glassware:** small rocks glass (single old-fashioned, about 200 ml), one large ice cube
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | straight rye whiskey, 40-43% | any straight rye at that strength; stronger bottles run too hot over one cube |
| 7.5 ml (1½ teaspoons) | sorghum syrup | pure sorghum syrup; or pure cane syrup. Measure it: half a teaspoon either way tips the balance |
| 5 ml (1 teaspoon) | Underberg | recommended; or another digestif bitters |
| 1 strip | orange peel | |

**method**
1. Spoon the sorghum syrup and the Underberg into the glass.
2. Pour in the rye and stir with a bar spoon until the syrup has disappeared into the whiskey, about fifteen seconds. Do it before the ice: once it's cold, the syrup clings to the spoon.
3. Add one large ice cube and stir for another twenty to thirty seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
4. Squeeze the strip of orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Stir the sorghum in first: once it's cold, it clings. Then tell one person you'll be there, ahead of time.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*This glass holds grocery-store bitters. A Brooklyn liquor shop wasn't supposed to sell them.*

**whoYouAre**
A friend asks if you can help on moving day. "Probably," you say, with a grin that convinces nobody. On the day you're the first one there, with a van you borrowed from someone you won't name, and you leave after the last box is in. People introduce you with a warning: don't believe a word they say. You've never minded the warning.

You don't say you'll be there, because saying it out loud is a leash to you, and breaking it would be worse than anything they could call you. So you keep the bar low and clear it every time. You'd rather surprise them than let them down. When something really matters, your friends stop asking who's sensible and call you. You're the proof that someone can be rough round the edges and completely dependable, and to them that beats a good name any day.

**yours**

1. In 2003, LeNell Smothers opened a wine and liquor shop at the far end of Van Brunt Street in Brooklyn, almost on the waterfront. One drinks writer jokes that if you wanted to hide a business from its customers, you could hardly have picked a better spot. Bartenders found it regardless. She'd filled it with what they were looking for: bourbons not distributed in New York, rye when hardly anyone stocked it, a rye bottled from Kentucky barrels she'd chosen herself, bitter Italian liqueurs, and bitters that local liquor rules said belonged in a grocery store. She stocked those anyway.

2. Most liquor shops didn't bother with bottles that sold slowly. She told that writer, in 2014, that she knew how hard many of those things were to find if you loved classic cocktails, and while friends in the trade worried about buying Hennessy by the case at a good price, she went after odd cases of amaro, the bitter liqueur Italy makes from herbs. She was famous for her shelves, and often just as famous for her temper. Being told off by her became almost an initiation for her regulars. The first time Damon Boelte walked in, he started peeling the tissue paper off one of her bottles of rye, and she yelled at him on the spot. Later, she hired him. He says people are amazed when he tells them he worked at LeNell's.

3. The shop, I like to think, was a lot like you. It looked like the last place you'd count on, with a sharp word waiting at the counter, and it had exactly what you came for. And the people she told off were the ones most devoted to the place. That's you, as far as I can see. You give people every reason to expect nothing, and then you're the one who's there. You never ask them to rely on you. They just find out they can.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a straight-rye Old-Fashioned. That's the great classic of whiskey, sugar and bitters, here with rye, the whiskey she stocked when hardly anyone did. I swapped the usual bitters for a teaspoon of Underberg bitters, as a nod to the rule she bent so her customers could have it. The sweetness is a spoon and a half of sorghum syrup, the pressed juice of sorghum stalks boiled down into syrup, because its sweetness sits well with rye. It's stirred over a single block of ice in a short, heavy glass, with orange peel twisted above it for its oils. Deep, dark, bitter at the edges, and exactly what you'd drive to the end of the street for.

5. Next time someone you'd go anywhere for has a big day coming, skip the grin and the "probably". Say yes, plainly, the week before. You won't lose an inch of your freedom: you were always going to go. What changes is theirs. For once they get to know, instead of hope. And you might find the warning was never what they believed about you.

**closing line:** Tomás's: *Stir the sorghum in first: once it's cold, it clings. Then tell one person you'll be there, ahead of time.* It agrees with y5's position (say it before), not the creed. y5 avoids "you'll be there" and "ahead of time", so the two don't repeat each other.

It is, and you know why, even if you seldom explain it. In a crisis, people watch whoever's in front to see how serious it is, and a rule that's still being kept tells them it isn't over. After Hurricane Katrina, Neal Bodenheimer, then tending bar in New York, felt he should be back in New Orleans. Many people from the city who lived elsewhere felt that if they didn't go home, the city might not survive. So he came home. His idea was to be one of the first there with a cocktail bar standing on its own, not inside a hotel or a restaurant. He bought a building in Freret, a lonely neighbourhood far from the French Quarter, and his partner, Matt Kohnke, loved it. At least ten to twenty people tried to talk him out of it: a terrible idea, they said. Years later he admitted that at first they'd been a little nervous too, and that they couldn't afford to be anywhere else. 2. Cure opened in 2009. He handed the drinks over to his bartenders. What he did give the bar was a dress code: no shorts, no flip-flops, no baseball caps. It gave the place a reputation it never quite lived down. For the first nine months to a year, he said, they spent their time persuading people that they should drink cocktails, and that the bar wasn't just pretentious. 3. Then comes my favourite part. Years later, talking about Cure's first days, he didn't say the critics had been wrong. He said craft cocktails had partly earned that label, and that they really had to work on their service. So they did. Cure did well from the start, and later he and his partners opened more bars. I like to think the dress code was never really about shorts. In what he called, in a way, a decaying city, where people started over, it said: this place still expects something of you. That's you. And the rest is you at your best: he granted the part of the criticism that was fair, worked on it, and kept going. 4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Brandy Crusta, a New Orleans classic from the mid-1800s. It's famous for how it's dressed: its name means the crust the sugar makes around the rim, and a long lemon peel lines the glass like a collar. Inside go cognac, a teaspoon apiece of dry curaçao (orange liqueur) and syrup, Angostura, and lemon, just half a teaspoon, all stirred until icy and strained into a little wineglass from the fridge, no ice in it: deep amber and rich. My main change is in the cognac. It sits for twenty minutes with ordinary black tea, so the firm grip at the end comes from the tea, not from more lemon. I did that as a nod to you: firm, without ever raising your voice. By 1908, one New York newspaperman was already sneering at sugar rims as old-fashioned. I kept the crust anyway. 5. Next time you're keeping a standard and someone calls it pretentious, or too much, don't hear it as all or nothing. Find the part they're right about, admit it plainly, and fix that part. # Pour — Leave It With Me · The Problem Solver (hero-sage)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Leave It With Me
- **tagline:** The plan's gone. Now it gets interesting.
- **glassware:** six small tumblers (about 180 ml), chilled in the freezer; a pitcher (about 1.5 litres)
- **contains:** `[]`
- **serves:** 6 (one pitcher, six small tumblers)

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 300 ml | white rum, light and dry (Spanish-style, unaged or lightly aged, 37.5-45%; not spiced, not sweetened) | the kind of rum that was there when the gin wasn't |
| 100 ml | fresh lime juice (about 3 to 4 limes), measured | |
| 50 g | caster sugar (granulated works, it takes longer) | dissolved in the lime, no syrup: rum, lime and sugar, nothing else |
| 4 | makrut lime leaves, fresh or frozen | lime's scent, without more sour; they come out before you pour |
| about 500 g | crushed ice (a bag of cubes in a tea towel, hit with a rolling pin) | |

**method**
1. Put six small tumblers in the freezer for 10 minutes.
2. Pour the lime juice into the pitcher, add the sugar, and stir until no grains are left on the bottom: about a minute.
3. Tear each makrut leaf in half and drop the halves into the lime. Press them against the bottom of the pitcher with a muddler or the end of a rolling pin, five times each, until they smell strongly of lime.
4. Add the rum.
5. Fill the pitcher about two-thirds with the crushed ice. Swizzle for 30 seconds by the clock: push a long spoon down to the bottom and work it up and down through the ice, turning it as you go.
6. Lift the leaves out with the spoon.
7. Pour straight away into the six tumblers, ice and all, along the row and back, so every glass gets the same.

**closingLine:** *Pour all six in one go, along the row and back. And the next time the plan falls apart, admit you're having fun.*
