## Reading

**epigraph**
*The first was made in a pitcher, a family story goes, when the gin ran out.*

**whoYouAre**
The oven gives up an hour before twelve people arrive. Someone says the evening's ruined, someone else starts looking up takeaways, and you're already at the open fridge, asking what you've got. You'd never wish it on anyone. But when the plan breaks and every face turns to you, a small part of you lights up. You keep that quiet. It hardly seems fair to enjoy someone else's emergency.

The bit you never mention is the blank before the answer comes. They're all looking at you, and there's nothing there yet. That blank is your nightmare, and somehow the whole fun of it too, because a puzzle that couldn't beat you wouldn't be worth solving. So you keep a level face through it, and no one learns how close it felt. The moment you ask what there is to work with, the room stops panicking and starts looking. Everyone gets something to do with their hands, and a little of your nerve. That's a real gift, and most people never notice who started it.

**yours**

1. In the 1890s, Jennings Cox ran an iron-mining company near Daiquirí, a port town in the east of Cuba. The family story goes that he had some American visitors to serve, and found he'd run out of gin. He did have rum, from a distillery in Santiago, under thirty miles away. But he worried, the family says, that it wouldn't suit the Americans' taste.

2. So, in the family's telling, he picked limes from a tree in his own garden, added their juice and some sugar to soften the rum, and swizzled it all in a pitcher with shaved ice. It went down well at once, the accounts say. One of his engineers later remembered it as more of a group effort among Cox and his crew, and maybe it was. People in the Caribbean had been mixing rum, limes and sugar for two centuries by then, but the Daiquiri, a renowned classic today, goes back to him: he made the first one, or at least oversaw its making. And for years afterwards, the old newspaper accounts say, he simply called it his rum sour, and kept taking it to the bars of Santiago.

3. I like to think none of his visitors saw the worry the family remembered. They saw a man with a pitcher and a handful of limes. I recognise you in that: the answer arrives with a level face, and the doubt stays behind it. And then there's the name. He'd solved a problem with visitors to serve, and for years he went on handing the answer round as just his rum sour. Whether he enjoyed that day isn't known, but I like to think he did. You'd do the same: you hand the answer over plainly, and nobody hears how much you loved finding it.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is built like that pitcher, for six: a Daiquiri in the shape the family story gives it. White rum and fresh lime, with sugar stirred into the lime until it's gone, swizzled on crushed ice for thirty seconds and poured straight away into six small chilled tumblers, so nobody waits longer than anyone else. A Daiquiri always asks for some quick thinking, because limes vary in sourness from one fruit to the next. I've measured everything a measure can fix, and the limes are yours to judge. My only addition is four makrut lime leaves, pressed into the lime and lifted out before you pour. Makrut is a different lime, with harsh juice but fragrant leaves, so the answer comes from the part of the tree you'd never think to squeeze. The leaves bring lime's scent without making the drink any sharper. They're there as one more answer to his worry, and as a nod to the question you always ask first: what else is there? It's icy, bright and fresh, and the lime carries right through it.

5. When every face next turns to you and nothing has come yet, tell them the truth, smiling: this is the bit you love most. Watch what that does. They stop waiting for you to produce an answer and start hunting with you, and the blank isn't yours alone any more. It becomes a game the whole room is playing, and you can love it in the open.

**closing line:** Tomás's (T1): *Pour all six in one go, along the row and back. And the next time the plan falls apart, admit you're having fun.* It agrees with y5's position and borrows none of y5's words.

# Pour — The First Guess · The Free Spirit (innocent-explorer)

## Cocktail

- **name:** The First Guess
- **tagline:** Your questions are how everyone else starts looking.
- **glassware:** a small tulip-shaped glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
- **contains:** `["spice"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 ml | VSOP cognac | any VSOP: by law it has spent at least four years in wood |
| 15 ml | cognac steeped with Sichuan peppercorns | made beforehand (see Method); it gives a faint tingle on the lips |
| 35 ml | Pineau des Charentes (white) | the Cognac region's own aperitif: grape juice stopped with young cognac before it could become wine, the cognac from the same farm, then rested in oak; any white Pineau |
| 1 | strip of lemon peel | squeezed over the top, then set aside |

**method**
1. Beforehand: lightly crush 1 level teaspoon of Sichuan peppercorns with the back of a spoon. Leave them in 60 ml of the cognac for 20 minutes, then strain them out. That makes enough for four drinks, and it lasts.
2. Put the glass in the freezer for 10 minutes.
3. Pour 30 ml cognac, 15 ml of the peppercorn cognac and 35 ml Pineau into a mixing glass or jar.
4. Fill it with ice and stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the jar is very cold.
5. Strain into the cold glass. No ice in the glass.
6. Hold the lemon peel over the drink, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the surface. Then set the peel aside.

**closingLine:** *Ask what's in it before anyone tells you what it is.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*From around Cognac, where something growing on the walls was misnamed for over a century.*

**whoYouAre**
When someone says "actually, nobody's really sure", most people sigh. You light up. You ask why: why the form needs that box, why a thing is called what it's called, why everyone does it this way. You're not making a point. You'd honestly like to know, and you're secretly hoping the answer will be stranger than you expected. It usually is.

Not everyone hears it that way. Over the years a few of your questions got you told off: "because I said so", the sigh, the look across the table. So now you ask lightly, with a smile, as if it hardly matters. It matters. The worst answer, to you, is a label: "oh, it's just a…", handed over to close the subject, so that nobody looks again. And yet around you, people do look again. With you, "I don't know" stops being embarrassing and becomes the start of the fun, and people need that more than they'll ever tell you.

**yours**

1. In 1872, a pharmacist in Cognac named Antonin Baudoin drew two botanists' attention to a black growth on the walls and roof tiles near the distilleries. It looked like soot. A few years later he printed his own short study of it. His answer was that it was a kind of blue-green algae. He was wrong.

2. Others filed it under a catch-all name that more than three hundred kinds of fungus have been put under over the years, nearly all of them moved out since. Then for decades the science went almost silent, and the studies that did look kept calling it the ordinary sort of fungus found everywhere. It wasn't. More than a century after Baudoin's first look, a team of scientists showed it didn't fit the group it had been put in, or any similar one, and gave it a group of its own, named after him, as the man who first brought it to scientists' attention. Its nearest known relatives live on rock in Antarctica. It feeds on the spirit that escapes ageing barrels, yet it's millions of years older than any barrel, so it's thought to live on something else too. Nobody is quite sure what.

3. I like to think Baudoin felt what you feel the moment someone says "it's just…": that it wasn't, quite. He wrote fifteen pages on it, and guessed wrong in print. Then the people who finally got it right put his name on it anyway. That's what your questions do. Even the ones that land wrong get other people looking, and what they find is often stranger than anyone guessed.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is stirred over ice until it's icy, then poured without it, the way a Martini is, from two bottles from around Cognac. One is a cognac aged for years in oak. The other is Pineau des Charentes, the region's aperitif: sweet grape juice stopped with young cognac from the same farm before it could become wine, then rested in oak too. Into part of the cognac I've steeped a few Sichuan peppercorns. You'll feel them as a faint tingle on your lips before the warmth comes through, a small question in the glass, the kind you've never been able to leave alone. I've poured it into a tulip-shaped glass, narrow at the top, to keep the scent with you. I like to think of it as a little of what escapes the barrels, kept for you this time.

5. So when a question next comes to you, don't make it small. Ask it properly, and offer your guess, even if you suspect it's wrong. Being wrong didn't keep Baudoin's name off it. It got the whole thing looked at. And I'd bet the real answer turns out stranger than your guess. That's the part you'll enjoy most.

# Pour — Straight Up · The Underdog (innocent-hero)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Straight Up
- **tagline:** You keep getting better, and never need someone else to lose.
- **glassware:** a thin stemmed coupe, chilled in the freezer
- **contains:** `["nuts"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 65 ml | borovička (a juniper spirit from Slovakia and the Czech Republic) | Or, if you can't find it, a juniper-led London dry gin. |
| 22.5 ml | fresh lime juice | |
| 17.5 ml | blended mango syrup (homemade, below) | Tropical fruit, the kind he brought into his drinks after a trip to London. Mango is related to cashew and pistachio, so if nuts are a worry, leave this one aside. |

**method**
1. The day before, or up to two weeks ahead, make the mango syrup. Weigh 250 g ripe, peeled mango flesh and 250 g white sugar, blend until smooth and the sugar has dissolved, then press it through a fine sieve. Keep it covered in the fridge.
2. Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
3. Pour the borovička, lime juice and mango syrup into a shaker. (Some borovičkas have a little sugar added: if yours tastes sweet on its own, use 15 ml of syrup.)
4. Fill it with ice, close it, and shake firmly for about twelve seconds, until the outside of the shaker is frosted.
5. Strain into the cold glass, through a small tea sieve to catch the ice chips. No garnish.

**closingLine:** *No garnish. And when good news comes, let it in first.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Mango and juniper, from far apart, have a note in common. It was always there.*

**whoYouAre**
You never set out to win anything. You wanted to get a little better at the thing in front of you, then a little better again. So you rarely turn round to see how far it has taken you. Other people do, and when they mention it, you're honestly surprised.

And when something good comes your way, there's a moment before the happiness. You replay how it happened, checking it was all fair, as if someone might ask. Somewhere along the road you learned that good things can be taken back, and you couldn't bear anyone thinking you hadn't got there honestly.

What you don't notice is that you never suspect anyone else. When someone you know gets the job or the prize, you're simply glad, and sure they got there fairly too. Not many people manage that, and it's a gift: people watch you take the straight road and start to believe it goes somewhere.

**yours**

1. It starts with a cocktail shaker. In 1994, the day after he saw the Tom Cruise film *Cocktail*, a Slovak named Stanislav Vadrna asked the boss of the village pub where he worked to buy him one. Later he wanted to work at a formal cocktail bar in Prague. He had long dreadlocks then, and the owner asked, "What about the hair?" He trimmed it back a bit. Then every weekend he rode the train five hours to Prague to work there as a barback, the bartender's helper, while running a restaurant in Slovakia during the week.

2. At Paparazzi in Bratislava, the bar he later ran, the menu changed with every trip he took: after London, out went the thick glassware and in came tropical fruit. When he wasn't travelling, he sat in internet cafés, translating articles about cocktails into Slovak. Then, on a whim, he posted his menu to a brand-new award in New Orleans. Two months after its first ceremony, a package arrived. He didn't know Paparazzi had won Best Cocktail Menu until he opened his mail.

3. A room in New Orleans knew before he did. Of all the places around the world where the cocktail revival took hold, the writer Robert Simonson calls Vadrna's the most improbable. I don't think any of it was luck. He learned from everyone he could reach, and the menu he sent was one he'd made himself. If it had been you opening that package, I suspect you'd have checked it twice, looking for the mistake. There wasn't one. That's your road too: no shortcut and no plan to win, only the next thing, done well, until other people notice.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a sour, of the same family as the Daiquiri, one of the most famous drinks there is. It's shaken, because the day after that film he asked for a shaker, and it goes into a thin, chilled glass. The base is borovička, a juniper spirit from the country he was born in. With it go lime and a mango syrup, as a nod to the tropical fruit he brought into Paparazzi after London. And here's what I love about it: mango and juniper have a piney note in common. The fruit comes from far away, and it tastes as if it had always been there. That's what happens to anything you learn by doing the work: it ends up yours.

5. So when something good finds you again, don't search it for the catch. You remember how you got there, and nobody handed you any of it. Someone near you is watching to see whether the long way pays off. Show them it does. The checking can wait, and I'd bet it never finds anything.

# Pour — There It Goes · The Giggler (innocent-jester)

## Cocktail

- **name:** There It Goes
- **tagline:** You find it funny first. Then everyone does.
- **glassware:** a coupe (about 180–200 ml), chilled
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22.5 ml (¾ oz) | bourbon | 43% or stronger |
| 22.5 ml (¾ oz) | Amaro Nonino Quintessentia, recommended | an Italian bitter herbal liqueur made on grappa (a brandy distilled from what's left after winemaking); or any other bitter herbal liqueur made on grappa |
| 22.5 ml (¾ oz) | Aperol, recommended | or any bright orange Italian bitter aperitif of about 11% |
| 20 ml | fresh lemon juice | a touch less than the printed recipe's ¾ oz, so it's bright, not sharp |
| 5 drops | salt water | 1 level teaspoon fine salt stirred into 4 teaspoons water; or a small pinch of fine salt |

**method**
1. Make the salt water once: stir 1 level teaspoon of fine salt into 4 teaspoons of warm water until it's clear. It keeps in the fridge for months.
2. Put the coupe in the freezer to chill.
3. Pour the bourbon, the Nonino, the Aperol and the lemon juice into a shaker. Add five drops of the salt water.
4. Fill the shaker three-quarters full with ice, close it and shake for about 12 seconds, until the shaker's too cold to hold comfortably.
5. Strain into the cold coupe. No garnish.

**closingLine:** *Five drops of salt water before you shake. And when something's funny, laugh out loud.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Behind this drink is one named for whatever song was on. One city adopted it.*

**whoYouAre**
A friend is halfway through a story, and you've already gone. Not a polite laugh: the real one, eyes watering, trying to say "sorry, go on" and not managing it. You're hardly ever the one telling the joke. You're the one who can't stop laughing at it, and that's usually the moment it gets funny for everybody else.

What people don't see is how many you hold in: in meetings, at the serious dinner, anywhere someone might think less of you for it. A laugh held in sits in your chest all afternoon. You've heard "you'd laugh at anything" more times than you can count. You wouldn't. You just find more of it funny. Now and then there's the second when you're the only one laughing and the room doesn't follow, and it stays with you longer than you let on. And the fear underneath is being told off for it so often that one day you stop. Please don't. When you laugh at something someone said, they leave feeling funny.

**yours**

1. In 2001, Sam Ross's family opened a cocktail bar in Fitzroy, in Melbourne, and called it Ginger. Most people who went remember it as inventive and odd: "lots of orange plastic", one bartender remembered, like "a psychedelic spaceship". Sebastian Reaburn, who worked there, said the menu "read like a comedy script". And Jacob Briars said the thing I love most about it: at Ginger, "there was no such thing as the idea anything might be wrong".

2. Not everyone was charmed, Sydney's bartenders least of all. In Reaburn's words, the place was all "so tongue in cheek", and "there was a credibility gap". Some years later, Ross made a drink for the opening menu of a new bar in Chicago, one where he never worked. It's called the Paper Plane, after a song by M.I.A. he had on while he was working it out. It became, he said, the second most travelled of his drinks, and Toronto took to it so completely that years later he called it "essentially the official drink of Toronto". Why Toronto, he couldn't say.

3. I like to think that's the Ginger in it. A whole city's bars joined in, and not even the man who made it could explain why. That's how your laugh works too. Nobody in the room decides to follow it. They just do. And I like to think the name suits it for one more reason, though it came from the song: a paper plane is the thing that sails across a room where everyone's being very serious, and somebody always smiles.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is the Paper Plane, a modern classic, with two small changes of mine. It's bourbon, Aperol (a bright orange Italian aperitif, gently bitter), Amaro Nonino (an Italian bitter herbal liqueur made on grappa, a brandy distilled from the grape skins, stems and seeds left once the juice is pressed out for wine) and fresh lemon. It's shaken until the shaker's uncomfortable to hold, and poured off the ice into a coupe that's been waiting in the freezer. I've taken a little of the lemon out, so it's bright rather than sharp. Then I've added five drops of salted water. It isn't meant to taste salty. It brings nothing of its own; it makes everything around it come forward, and it takes the frown off the bitter. I put it there for you, because that's what your laugh does for other people's jokes.

5. Next time something's funny in a room that's gone stiff, don't hold it in. Look round first: there's nearly always someone else trying not to laugh. Let yours go, and you'll have given them theirs. Then enjoy it. It really was funny.

# Pour — The Big Words · The Teenage Heart-throb (innocent-lover)

## Cocktail

- **name:** The Big Words
- **tagline:** You've never loved anything a little.
- **glassware:** a cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | aged Jamaican rum, about 50% (any aged Jamaican rum from 40% to 57% works; not spiced) | the style and strength of the rum in the Brooklyn Club's drink, as the *Eagle* printed it in 1945 |
| 30 ml | sweet vermouth (Italian style) | the club poured as much vermouth as rum; at half the rum the drink stays bright |
| 7.5 ml | Amaro CioCiaro (*recommended*), or any dark, bittersweet Italian amaro (herbal liqueur) with a burnt-orange taste, about 30% | in place of the 1908 Brooklyn's French orange bitter, Amer Picon; the stand-in Oxford and *Imbibe!* both name |
| 1 dash | Angostura bitters | the club's dash |
| 1 | wide strip of peel from a fresh, thick-skinned orange, about 2.5 cm across | squeezed high over the top, then dropped in |

**method**
1. Put the cocktail glass in the freezer for 10 minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
2. With a small knife, cut a wide strip of peel from a fresh, thick-skinned orange, about 2.5 cm across, leaving a little of the white underneath so it holds its shape.
3. Fill a mixing glass or a jar with ice. Pour in the rum, the vermouth, the CioCiaro and the dash of bitters.
4. Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
5. Empty the cocktail glass and strain the drink into it.
6. Hold the peel by its edges, orange side down, high above the glass (about a hand's width), and squeeze it sharply so its oils fall in a fine spray over the drink.
7. Rub the orange side around the rim and drop the peel in.

**closingLine:** *Squeeze the peel from high up, so nobody misses it. If they laugh, keep the words the same size.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Manhattan has a cocktail. So does the Bronx. Brooklyn is still asking.*

**whoYouAre**
When you love something, people hear about it. A person, a band, a team, the town you grew up in: it gets all of you, out loud, usually before anyone has asked. You're the one who makes the playlist, writes the birthday card that runs onto the back, and says the big words before anyone else dares to.

People assume you don't notice how it looks. You do. Nobody knows the pause after the big words better than you: the half-second before the room decides whether to smile with you or at you. You step into it regardless. The part you hide is the walk home afterwards, going back over the one face that smirked. What stings is being laughed at for meaning it, because it tempts you to say it a little smaller next time. Still, there's a gift in it: everyone you love has proof. Most people go their whole lives without being loved out loud, in front of others. Whoever you love never has to wonder.

**yours**

1. Manhattan had a cocktail, and so did the Bronx, so for well over a century Brooklyn has wanted one of its own. The earliest on record is from 1883, a rum Manhattan made at the Brooklyn Club, and it apparently never left the club. In 1908 Jack Grohusko, a Manhattan bartender, printed a Brooklyn in the book he wrote. He never lived in Brooklyn. The man who owned his restaurant did.

2. In the summer of 1910, the papers reported, a man living in Brooklyn couldn't sleep, so he got up and mixed a new one: a long glass of cider, absinthe and ginger ale. Asked what excuse he had for calling a pint a cocktail, Maurice Hegeman said there was no law about it, and that he wanted Brooklyn to have a cocktail people would recognise it by. That September, papers from Kansas City to Washington printed another Brooklyn, someone else's, offered with a very flowery tribute, and bartenders had their fun with its recipe. One of the Waldorf-Astoria's bartenders said all it was missing was the ice cream. A bartender far from Broadway said that if he lived in Brooklyn, he'd stick to beer.

3. Brooklyn kept at it. In 1945 the Bronx borough president teased that Brooklyn still had no cocktail, and offered one made with vinegar and DDT. Brooklyn answered so fast that within days the *Eagle*'s columnist heard thirty-three recipes in a single day, and gave up on the subject because more kept coming. Bartenders today are still naming new ones after Brooklyn's neighbourhoods.

4. That, to me, is you. Not the winning, because no Brooklyn has ever really stuck. The not stopping. I like to think Hegeman knew exactly how a pint of cider and ginger ale sounded when he called it a cocktail, and said it plainly because he meant it. When someone laughed, sooner or later somebody else in Brooklyn picked it up, at full size.

5. The cocktail I've made for you is a close relation of the Manhattan, that renowned classic so many other cocktails grew from. It starts from the Brooklyn Club's drink as the *Brooklyn Eagle* printed it in 1945: strong Jamaican rum with Italian vermouth, plus Angostura bitters, just one dash. The club poured equal measures of the two; mine is an aged Jamaican rum, two parts to one of vermouth, so it stays bright. Where Grohusko's had a little French bitter made from orange peel, mine has a bar spoon and a half of a dark, bittersweet Italian liqueur that tastes of burnt orange. It's stirred cold, rich and warm from the rum, with a bitter-orange edge, poured into an ice-cold cocktail glass. The last touch is mine too: a wide orange peel, squeezed high over the top, so the orange arrives before anything else. As a nod to you, a drink built on the club's quiet Brooklyn now announces itself.

6. Whenever you say the big words and somebody laughs, don't take them back, and don't trim them for next time. Same words, same size. Somebody usually joins in. In Brooklyn, it was thirty-three recipes in a day.

# Pour — Fresh Air · The Outsider (innocent-outlaw)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Fresh Air
- **tagline:** You know what enough feels like, and make it look like freedom.
- **glassware:** a heavy tumbler (about 300 ml), two or three small lumps of ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 45 ml | aged rum (not spiced, about 40%) | rum was the Stone Fence's original spirit, before whisky |
| 120 ml | dry, still farmhouse cider, the sharpest you can find (about 5-6%) | not sweet, not sparkling. Small, sharp wild apples were thought to make the best cider, Thoreau wrote, though he still begrudged them to the cider-mill |
| 2 or 3 | small lumps of ice | as Jerry Thomas asked for in 1862 |
| 1 thin slice | raw sharp apple, skin on (a crab apple, or the sourest apple to hand) | the apple he'd rather have eaten in the field: raw, cut last |

**method**
1. Keep the cider cold in the fridge until you need it.
2. Drop two or three small lumps of ice into a heavy tumbler and pour in the rum.
3. Pour the cider in slowly over the ice, and give it one turn with a spoon.
4. Cut one thin slice from the sharpest apple you have, skin on, and slip it into the glass last.

**closingLine:** *Carry it out of doors before you taste it. Whoever follows you out will understand.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*In 1862 a famous bar book printed this drink with sweet cider. Others kept pouring it tart.*

**whoYouAre**
At a wedding or a birthday, someone asks what you're up to these days. You tell them: the same place, the work you like, your usual walk in the morning. Then you watch them wait politely for the rest. There isn't any rest. Years ago you stepped out of the race everyone else is running, quietly, and you don't miss it.

Living with less was easy. Being loved by people who think you're wasting yourself is harder. "You could do so much more." They mean it kindly, which is why you don't argue. And under that sits a quieter fear. No one will drag you back in. But someone kind might ask, with a job you'd be good at or a favour "just for a while", and once you're back indoors, the part of you they liked would turn sour.

After an afternoon with you, they go home wanting a little less, and lighter for it. You make "enough" look like a choice, not a defeat, and you show them someone can say no and stay kind.

**yours**

1. In late autumn, the writer Henry David Thoreau went into old pastures for the small, sharp apples farmers left out as unsalable. To someone out walking, he wrote, they were the choicest fruit. Indoors, he wrote, it tasted like another fruit: one he took out of his desk was "sour enough to set a squirrel's teeth on edge". There, he wrote, you miss the November air, "which is the sauce it is to be eaten with".

2. He knew he was describing himself: "one thought for the field, another for the house". His friend Emerson couldn't help "counting it a fault in him that he had no ambition": instead of engineering for all America, he was "the captain of a huckleberry party". Emerson meant it. In the same sketch, Emerson also wrote: "He chose to be rich by making his wants few, and supplying them himself."

3. As Thoreau tells it, nothing in the apple changes when it's carried in. Only the room does. You know that about yourself, so you keep turning down the bigger room, however kindly it's offered. Emerson wrote that it cost Thoreau nothing to say no. It costs you something every time, because you like the people asking. You're not hiding from anyone. You simply know where you're at your best. And I like to think the ones asking are curious about the world as you see it, and don't know how to say so.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Stone Fence, a drink from colonial America, on record under another name by 1750. I went back to its older pairing of rum and hard cider, and kept it sharp: aged rum and a dry, still farmhouse cider, the sharpest you can find, over two or three small lumps of ice, with no sugar to soften it, because sharp was never a fault that needed fixing. Thoreau wrote that wild apples like his were thought to make the best cider, though he still begrudged them to the cider mill. So, for the apples he'd rather have eaten in the field, a thin slice of raw, sharp apple goes in at the end.

5. You don't owe anyone a bigger life, or an explanation of this one. Thoreau once kept a smooth face while tempting a companion with one of those sour apples. By winter, when frost and thaw had turned them sweet, the two of them were filling their pockets together. So stop defending your life to the ones who worry about you. Have one of them come along. Some will taste what you taste, and you'll have someone to fill your pockets with.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*This drink was never poured for one.*

**whoYouAre**
You believe the best of people, and you'd rather be disappointed now and then than live any other way. You forgive quickly. It isn't that you don't notice. It's that holding on to it costs more than it's worth. When things go wrong for someone, you don't make a speech. You just stay. People feel safer around you, and they often couldn't tell you why, they just do.

Here's the part you struggle to show: you worry about being the one left out, the one who said the wrong thing, the one who let somebody down. So you make sure nobody else ever has to feel that way.

**yours** (authored base; the live tailoring keeps these paragraphs, anchors and order)

1. Nobody knows exactly where punch was born. What we do know is that in the 1600s, English traders in India were mixing the local spirit with water, sugar, citrus and spice, and that sailors carried the habit to every port they reached. For almost two hundred years, a shared bowl of punch was the drink of choice across much of the world. It was the first mixed drink with spirits to travel the globe, and it's the ancestor of drinks you know, like the Daiquiri and the Margarita.
2. Even its name is a small mystery. The story most people tell is that "punch" comes from the Hindi word for five, for its five ingredients. Maybe. But one of the first Englishmen to write the drink down, a merchant in India around 1630, recorded it under a Hindi name that means "four shares". I like to think that's the truer name: not what goes into it, but how many people get some.
3. Punch was never a drink for one. It was made in a bowl and passed around. Small bowls went from hand to hand, in taverns and grand houses alike, and anyone in the room could drink. Some bowls even had words painted inside that only appeared once everyone had had their share: "Drink fair." "One bowl more." That's you, isn't it? You're the one who makes sure the bowl comes round to everybody, and that nobody is left standing at the edge of the room.
4. So I made your punch the old way, the way that takes time, to honour the time you give to others. It starts the night before: strips of lemon peel buried in sugar and left alone until the sugar has drawn out all their oil and turned into a fragrant syrup. You can't rush it. You can only give it time. Then lemon juice, a bottle of aged rum and cold black tea, poured over one big block of ice and ladled into cups. It isn't clever. It's generous. It's a drink that says "I was thinking of you yesterday."
5. Here's what I'd ask of you. Make this one day for people you love, and don't wait for a reason. And the next time you're the one who's struggling, let someone pass the bowl to you. You've spent a long time making sure nobody is left out. You're allowed to be looked after too.

# Pour — Just So You Know · The Wise Kid (innocent-sage)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Just So You Know
- **tagline:** You tell people what you'd want to be told.
- **glassware:** a small stemmed sour glass (about 180 ml), chilled in the freezer, no ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | bourbon | any bourbon of 40 to 46%; not bottled-in-bond or barrel proof |
| 20 ml | fresh lemon juice | from half a medium lemon, measured |
| 2 1/2 tsp (about 11 g) | white sugar | granulated, pressed into the squeezed lemon half |

**method**
1. Put the sour glass in the freezer for 10 minutes.
2. Cut a lemon in half. Squeeze one half and measure 20 ml of juice into the shaker.
3. Cut the squeezed half into four pieces and drop them in with the sugar. Press them with a muddler (or the end of a rolling pin) until the sugar is wet and smells of lemon. Press, don't grind: shredded white pith turns bitter.
4. Add the bourbon, fill the shaker with ice and shake well for about 12 seconds.
5. Strain into the cold glass through the shaker's strainer and a small kitchen sieve, so no peel or sugar grains get through.
6. Hold it by the stem, so your hand doesn't warm it.

**closingLine:** *Press the sugar into the peel until it smells of lemon. One little step, and the whole glass is fresher.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A Whiskey Sour, as it was ordered. For a while, one bartender made it with Scotch.*

**whoYouAre**
There's a crumb on someone's chin at dinner, or a typo on the first slide that everyone has already read, or a colleague whose name someone has been saying wrong for a year. Most people saw it. Maybe they thought it wasn't their place, or that it was kinder to leave it. You go over, quietly, and say so, to that person and nobody else. It never felt brave to you. It just seemed like what you'd want, if it were you.

There's a second after that you never mention. You've said it, and for a second you wait to see whether you're in trouble. At some point someone told you the truth was rude, and part of you still listens for it. And what hurts more is the reverse: finding out that people you trust watched you get something wrong and said nothing, to be nice.

Your way hands people the chance to fix it while it's still small, and it counts for a lot. Being told by you never feels like being caught out. It's being trusted to take it.

**yours**

1. Gary Regan was a bartender from England who later wrote a book on making drinks. He turns up more than once in my stories; this one I keep for you. In the book he tells newcomers to expect mistakes, and gives one of his own. Once he had a job behind a bar, for a while, whenever someone ordered a Whiskey Sour, he made a Scotch Sour. In England, ask for whisky and you get Scotch. The Whiskey Sour is an American classic, and in his book it's made with bourbon or rye.

2. No customer put him right. Maybe none of them noticed, he writes, "Or if they did, they certainly didn't tell me." A waitress caught it. That's all he says about her: no name, no words. Only that until she did, he hadn't learned what he was doing wrong.

3. Whoever else noticed, if anyone did, let him carry on. I like to think she did him the kind of favour you do, and treated him as someone who could take it. "Caught" is his word, but he doesn't use it as a complaint: he set the story down in print, against himself, for anyone starting out. That's what you rarely get to see after you've said it: the mistake fixed, then handed on to whoever comes next.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is the drink that was ordered, a Whiskey Sour: bourbon, sugar and fresh lemon, a renowned classic, served chilled, in a small stemmed glass. It borrows one tip from the same book: granulated sugar pressed into the lemon. The sugar works at the peel, he wrote, and the drink tastes fresher for it. I did it as a nod to what follows a catch like hers. He was put right, and then he passed on something better. Telling someone doesn't end with them being fixed. Sometimes it's how they get good.

5. So when you spot the next one, say it, and don't stand there waiting for the verdict. I'd bet most people are glad, even if it takes them years to get round to saying so. And you've done this for plenty of people without ever asking for it back. Pick someone close and ask them to do the same for you. It's your turn to be told.

# Pour — Anyway · The Morale Booster (jester-caregiver)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Anyway
- **tagline:** You decide it's going to be a good night. Then you make it one.
- **glassware:** stemmed wine glass (about 250 ml), chilled
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml (2 oz) | London dry gin, 43% or stronger | coriander is one of the usual botanicals in a London dry gin |
| 30 ml (1 oz) | sweet vermouth (Italian style) | more of the sweet than Oxford's recipe: it puts back the sugar a pour of orange juice would bring |
| 1 teaspoon (5 ml) | dry vermouth | |
| 1 thin wheel | fresh orange, about ½ cm thick, cut into eight pieces, peel and all | the peel is where most of an orange's flavour is; the thin wheel gives only a splash of juice |
| ¼ teaspoon | coriander seeds, lightly cracked | one of the usual flavourings in London dry gin, with a lemony note of its own; strained out before serving |
| 2 dashes | Peychaud's bitters, recommended (or another bright-red New Orleans-style aromatic bitters) | the Sazerac's bitters, for the guests who'd rather have had a Sazerac |

**method**
1. Put the wine glass in the freezer for ten minutes.
2. Cut a thin wheel from an orange, about half a centimetre, and cut it into eight pieces. Leave the peel on.
3. Put the orange pieces and the coriander seeds in a shaker. Press them firmly with a muddler (or the end of a rolling pin) until the peel smells strongly of orange and the juice runs.
4. Add the gin, both vermouths and the bitters. Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
5. Pour it through the shaker's strainer and a small tea strainer held over the glass, so no seeds or pulp get in.
6. Nothing on the rim. The orange is already in it.

**closingLine:** *Muddle the whole wheel, peel and all. Then tell the story of the one that didn't take.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*People tried everything to fix the orange in the Bronx cocktail. This is one more try.*

**whoYouAre**
It's a grey week, or a long wait, or a birthday nobody's quite in the mood for, and you've decided it's going to be good anyway. So you think of something: a silly game with proper rules, a theme, a time to turn up. Half the fun is that you took it seriously. People who would never start anything themselves find they've joined in, and even the one who swore they wouldn't ends up laughing.

There's a list, though, and only you have it: the ones that didn't take. The quiz nobody got into. The evening that stayed flat however hard you pushed it. Everyone else forgot them by the next morning. You didn't, because under all the fun is the thing you dread most: a gloom nobody could lift, and you the one who couldn't lift it. Even on the flat nights, people could tell that someone wanted the evening to be good for them. That's what your fun was for all along, and it matters more than whether the game worked.

**yours**

1. Early in 1917, on a Sunday afternoon in St. Louis, Clara Bell Walsh had about fifty guests over for something new: an hour of cocktails, from noon until one. A newspaper at the time gave her the credit for the idea. It's the first party on record that was planned as a cocktail party and called one.

2. It wasn't her first idea. She'd tried other party themes before it, and in one of them the guests dressed up as babies and drank from bottles. That one didn't catch on. The cocktail party did, and more than a century later it's still one of the ways people get together. I'd have gone to both.

3. It's the cocktail party people remember. But it might never have come without the ones before it, and I like to think she knew it. It's the same with the list you keep. The flat evenings on it aren't the opposite of the good ones. They're how you learned what people will join in with, and what they won't. And among the drinks that Sunday there were a few Sazeracs, served to the older guests who were set in their ways. I like to think that was someone making sure even the hardest ones to win over had something there for them. That's you, too.

4. The cocktail I've made for you starts from the sensation of her day, the Bronx: gin, two kinds of vermouth and orange. It was on her menu, and it was famously hard to get right. Put in enough orange juice to taste it, and the drink goes weak, so people kept trying new answers. The version I start from doesn't pour juice at all: one thin slice of orange is crushed in the shaker, peel and all, because the peel is where most of an orange's flavour is. You can taste the orange without drowning the gin. Then I added mine. A pinch of cracked coriander seeds goes in with the orange: coriander is one of the usual flavourings in London dry gin, with a lemony note of its own. And in place of the Angostura there are two dashes of Peychaud's, the Sazerac's bitters, for the guests who'd rather have had a Sazerac.

5. So keep the list. Just stop reading it as a record of what went wrong. Every idea on it that didn't take is part of the one that will. When something you've planned falls flat, laugh about it with them, and start planning another. Throw it anyway. I'd come to both.

# Pour — For Kicks · The Wacky One (jester-creator)

## Cocktail

- **name:** For Kicks
- **tagline:** You take a joke further than anyone, until everyone else is in on it.
- **glassware:** coupe, chilled
- **contains:** `["nuts"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 ml (1 oz) | blended scotch whisky | one country |
| 30 ml (1 oz) | Irish whiskey | and another, half and half, the way Harry's book has it |
| 22.5 ml (¾ oz) | fresh lemon juice | a little more than his book's sixth, which leaves the drink short of sour |
| 17.5 ml (3½ teaspoons) | orgeat (almond syrup) | his book's own note says it's made from almonds |
| 3 | whole roasted coffee beans | the fly: floated on top, never stirred in |

**method**
1. Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
2. Pour the scotch, the Irish whiskey, the lemon juice and the orgeat (the almond syrup) into a shaker.
3. Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about ten seconds.
4. Strain it into the cold coupe.
5. Drop three coffee beans onto the middle of the drink. They float on the thin froth the shaking leaves. They're there for the eye and the nose. Bite one if you like.

**closingLine:** *Three flies, every time. If you ever stop, start again at three.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Three coffee beans float on top. They're meant to be flies. It's a long story.*

**whoYouAre**
Somebody once said something daft in passing, and you didn't let it go. You took it one step further, then another. Now there's a word people use without knowing it started with you, a thing you always wear, a little ritual nobody remembers agreeing to. It started as a joke, and it's still a joke. You just never saw a reason to stop.

At every age, someone has expected you to grow out of it. What you don't say is that you could. Normal isn't a mystery to you: you could do it tomorrow, and nobody would stop you. That's the part that frightens you, more than any look across a room: how quietly it could happen. Meanwhile, next to you, other people get to be a bit ridiculous too, and they are. They feel freer around you than they'd ever think to tell you. That's a bigger gift than being taken seriously.

**yours**

1. The way a Paris bar's own book tells it, it started in 1924 with a gloomy piece by a New York columnist, who called the regulars of the Paris bars barflies: the ones who never seem to leave. His name, and this is true, was Oscar Odd McIntyre. Then a nightclub owner joked about it in an advert: his Christmas Eve takings would go to the "needy barflies".

2. Harry McElhone, a Scot who ran that bar, Harry's New York Bar, answered with an advert of his own, calling a meeting, and around Christmas the International Bar Flies was founded there. The book lists McIntyre as president, "Big Blue Bottlefly", and Harry as "Little Blue Bottlefly". By 1927 it had over five thousand members, and branches, called traps, from Shanghai to Buenos Aires. My guess is they joined for the reason people join in with you: someone had gone first, and was clearly fine.

3. The joke wasn't his. He just wouldn't let it end where most people would have, which is exactly what you do with a joke. And he kept it going. In 1940, as the war closed in, he locked his papers in a safe, buried it and left. After the war he returned to the bar and picked up where he left off, and a later booklet lists him as the society's president: "Exalted Blue Bottle Fly". He'd been promoted. I like to think the silliness was one of the things he kept safe.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is my take on Cameron's Kick, a forgotten classic, a whisky sour that first appeared in Harry's 1922 book. It's half Scotch whisky and half Irish whiskey, shaken with lemon and orgeat, a sweet almond syrup. Two countries' whiskies in one glass sounds like it shouldn't work, and it plainly does. I've given it a little more lemon than the old printed recipe, and a touch more almond, so it tastes brighter. Then I added the flies: three coffee beans floated on top, the way sambuca, an anise liqueur, is often served "with the fly", because with a little imagination the beans look like houseflies. Here they're for the Bar Flies. They add a little roasted-coffee scent as the glass comes up, and if you bite one, a bitter crunch against the almond.

5. Some stretches of your life will need you to be serious, and when one comes, you'll manage it. It doesn't get to take the silliness with it. When it's over, pick up where you left off: the word, the ritual, the thing you always wear, all of it. You won't be the only one who missed it.

**As the guest (the Wacky One).** *For Kicks* is how I'd explain any of it, and the drink's name is tucked inside, which is my kind of joke. The tagline and whoYouAre now agree. My word is out there, used by people who don't know it started with me, and that's the moment I secretly love. The epigraph stands cold: flies, a bartender, "it's a long story". whoYouAre ¶1 has no apology in it ("it's still a joke"). ¶2 names the fear I've never said aloud, how quietly I could turn normal, then says plainly what I give. The line: **"Normal isn't a mystery to you: you could do it tomorrow, and nobody would stop you."** The story's escalation is exactly my kind of daft: a gloomy article, a joke advert, then an actual meeting and "Little Blue Bottlefly". ### Names considered

provisional

- ***For Kicks*** (**the pick, settled with Wren in round 6**; mine in round 4). It's what the person does: nonsense for the pleasure of it (the persona's own story line), and "for kicks" is how people say they did something daft just because. It carries the drink's own name, Cameron's Kick, so the classic is recognised without being spelled out. It's easy to say across a bar ("A For Kicks, please") and makes the bartender smile. It doesn't repeat Wren's tagline direction ("You made it up. Now everyone says it."). Registry: no "Kicks". One near thing, owned: *For Good* (the Innovator, Explorer family) also opens with "For"; not a sibling.
- ***Not a Phase*** (Wren's round-4 pick; I conceded to it in round 5, then she struck it). It answers "you'll grow out of it" with a grin. But, as Wren caught, "it's not a phase" is what many people heard when they came out. Borrowing it for silliness could sting a guest for whom it isn't funny. It also only repeats the tagline and whoYouAre ¶2.
- ***Fly in It***: the joke you keep telling ("there's a fly in it"). It's loud and daft, but it names the garnish, not the person, and ordering it sounds like a complaint.
- ***Little Blue Bottlefly***: the title the 1927 book lists him under (F6, "listed as"). It's the most ridiculous and the most the person's. Two cautions: it captions Harry rather than the guest, and a bluebottle is a blowfly, which isn't a thought you want near a drink.
- ***Trap One***: the first branch, in his bar (F20). It's short and a little mysterious, but "trap" on a menu reads as a trick, which is the Trickster's ground.

In the spring of 2011, a bar opened in Chicago with no bar in it. There was no counter to lean on: the drinks came to the table, from stations at the back that looked more like a laboratory. A critic that first spring watched the server crack the ice and counted it among the drinks played, quietly, for laughs. The same review found the drinks could feel a little cold, because nobody had time to talk about them. Funny and cold, in the same week. In the summer of 2012 Charles Joly took over the drinks, and he said later it hadn't felt like a bar: it lacked a sense of hospitality. He didn't make the drinks ordinary. They stayed every bit as strange, but now a bartender came with them, to joke and to talk. It had to be, in his words, about "hospitality, the booze and a good time." 3. I like to think that critic put a finger on exactly the thing you worry about. The strange part was never the problem. The joke was there from the first week, and somebody laughed. What was missing was someone staying in the room with it. You know that second better than anyone, the one where people don't yet know whether they're allowed to laugh. It's a better second with someone beside them in it. 4. The cocktail I've made for you brings that idea home. Inside is the renowned classic, a rye Old-Fashioned: rye, demerara sugar, Angostura bitters and orange peel. It's a drink with as many recipes as bartenders, and the whole craft of it is restraint, so it's made exactly. It waits, cold and already diluted, in a shell of ordinary cloudy ice from your own freezer. A home freezer can't freeze a drink that strong, so plain ice holds it like a cup. Whoever made it cracks the shell at the table with one tap of a spoon, while whoever it's for looks on, and the drink runs out over its own broken ice. Nothing in the bottle is strange. The joke is all in how it arrives, which, if you ask me, is you exactly. 5. So keep every strange thing you had planned. Don't explain it beforehand, and don't make it sensible. Just don't disappear straight after. Stay for the second that follows, and for the conversation after that. Nobody needed the joke taken apart. They needed someone in it with them. # Pour — Off the Tour · The Naïf (jester-innocent)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Off the Tour
- **tagline:** Nobody believes your stories. They all happened.
- **glassware:** tall Collins glass (about 350 ml), crushed ice, the swizzle stick left standing in it, no straw
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | white rum, a flavourful one (about 40%) | Wondrich's advice for this drink: "a flavorful white one" |
| 25 ml | fresh lime juice (about one lime) | measure it: 30 ml makes it too sharp |
| 20 ml | simple syrup (1:1, white sugar and water) | |
| 5 ml (1 barspoon) | green absinthe steeped with tangerine peel (method, step 1) | the green in the Green Swizzle. Use one barspoon, no more |
| 4 dashes | Angostura bitters, dashed on top at the end | a dark-red band over the green |
| 1 | wooden swizzle stick, left standing in the glass | no stick? a bar spoon does the same job |

**method**
1. **Two days ahead, make the tangerine absinthe.** Peel one tangerine thinly with a vegetable peeler, orange skin only, none of the white. Put the peel in a small clean jar with 100 ml green absinthe (the wormwood-forward kind) and close it. Leave it two days somewhere cool, and shake it once a day. Strain it and bottle it. A barspoon makes one drink, so the bottle makes about twenty.
2. Make crushed ice. Wrap a tray of ice cubes in a clean tea towel and bash it with a rolling pin until it's nearly snow.
3. Pour the rum, lime, syrup and one barspoon of the tangerine absinthe into the tall glass.
4. Fill the glass about four-fifths with crushed ice.
5. Stand the swizzle stick in the drink with its prongs at the bottom. Hold the handle between flat palms and rub your hands back and forth so the stick spins, moving it slowly up and down. Keep going until the outside of the glass turns white with frost, about 20 to 30 seconds.
6. Pack more crushed ice on top until it mounds over the rim. Dash the Angostura over the ice. Leave the stick in the glass.

**closingLine:** *Spin the stick between your palms until the glass goes white. Then go back for whatever you were hurried past.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A Green Swizzle, Wembley, 1924. In a story, Bertie Wooster vowed to name a son after it.*

**whoYouAre**
You're somewhere you're meant to sit still: a hotel breakfast with its little rules, a waiting room, the long middle of a speech. Ten minutes, and something small has caught you. The sachet that won't tear. The toaster that sends the bread round twice. You give it all your attention, because right then it's the only problem in the world. It all goes sideways, and nobody there forgets how. You look up, and that's when you find the room.

You never set out to be funny. The part you laugh off is the hush: the "not now", the hand on your arm. Being told to sit still has always sounded like being told to be less, and what you dread is managing it, and nothing happening at all. Hushing you would cost everyone else their best stories, the dull mornings they still tell, fondly, years later. And after you, nobody needs to pretend the rules made sense.

**yours**

1. In 1924, at Wembley, the West Indies pavilion of the British Empire Exhibition poured the Green Swizzle. P. G. Wodehouse put Bertie Wooster there that year, in a story, tagging along with a friend who was being taken round to have his mind broadened. At lunch, every joke Bertie started had been stopped by a stare, and the one he finished got a waggled eyebrow. Now it's a stuffed fish and a jar of seeds, and exhibitions, he admits, have never been his thing.

2. Then, rushed past a bar, he spots a man stirring long, icy glasses with a stick, and the urge to see more of him won't go away. He and his friend slip away to it, and the moment the barman tells him what they're called, Bertie vows that any son of his will be named Green Swizzle Wooster.

3. For years, the Green Swizzle itself was taken for fiction. It wasn't: old newspapers show it was real, and for a while quite popular in the Caribbean.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Green Swizzle, a Caribbean classic, rebuilt from the parts listed for an old Trinidad bottled base, discontinued decades ago. Mine are white rum, fresh lime and sugar. The green comes from a barspoon of green absinthe, a spirit made with wormwood, that I steep with tangerine peel for two days. The tangerine is a travel writer's tip for the old wormwood bitters, passed on by a drinks historian; I borrowed it for the absinthe, and I put it in for you: the bright thing that turns up in the middle of something grim. Then the stick does the stirring. You give it your whole attention for about half a minute, and the glass tells you when to stop. It comes out tall, pale and very cold, with four dashes of Angostura on top, and it gets gentler as you go.

5. I like to think you'd have seen the man with the stick before anyone else on the tour did, and stopped. Next time you're being steered past the one thing you'd actually like to see, look round for the other person who's had about enough. There usually is one. Go together. Give it all your attention, and if something wonderful comes of it, make a promise far too big for it. Somebody will be telling that afternoon for years, and it'll all be true.

**Glass and drink:** a tall, straight Collins glass, its outside frosted white, packed with crushed ice mounded above the rim. # Pour — I'll Tell You Later · The Tease (jester-lover)

## Cocktail

- **name:** I'll Tell You Later
- **tagline:** You know how to make the waiting part of the pleasure.
- **glassware:** two demitasse cups (small coffee cups, about 90 ml) on saucers, warmed with hot water first
- **contains:** `["nuts"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 ml | VS cognac | steeped a few hours ahead with the peels and cinnamon |
| 15 ml | kirsch (clear, unsweetened cherry brandy) | steeped with the cognac; two parts cognac to one of kirsch, as in Oxford's recipe |
| 1 strip each | lemon peel and orange peel, no white pith | steeped in the spirits, then lifted out |
| half | cinnamon stick, broken into pieces | steeped in the spirits, then lifted out |
| 17.5 ml | demerara syrup (equal weights demerara sugar and water) | warmed with the spirits |
| 1 | orange-peel spiral (half an orange, cut round in one long strip), studded with 6 cloves | the warm spirits run down it into the cups |
| 100 ml | hot coffee with chicory (New Orleans style; or any dark-roast filter coffee), freshly made | added at the end, 50 ml a cup, by someone else |

**method**
1. A few hours ahead (3 to 4 is plenty), put the lemon and orange peel strips and the broken half cinnamon stick in a small jar with the cognac and kirsch. Close it and leave it.
2. When you're nearly ready, make the coffee and keep it hot. Fill the two cups with hot water to warm them. Cut the orange spiral and push the 6 cloves into it.
3. Lift the peels and cinnamon out of the jar. Pour the spirits and the syrup into a small pan and warm them over a low heat until they just steam, under a minute. Never let it bubble, and never light it.
4. Empty the cups. Hold the clove spiral over the first cup on a fork and pour half the warm spirits slowly down it, so they run over the peel and the cloves. Do the same over the second cup.
5. Hand the coffee to someone else. They pour 50 ml into each cup, whenever they like. Stir once and drink it hot.

**closingLine:** *Run the brandy down the peel. Then give someone else the coffee, and let the timing be theirs.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A New Orleans coffee that keeps you waiting for the coffee.*

**whoYouAre**
You've had the best news of your week since lunchtime, and you haven't said a word. It can wait until the plates are cleared. The present comes out last, after a decoy that gets a groan. Someone asks why you're smiling, you say "I'll tell you later", and they lean closer. The real pleasure is watching it reach their faces.

You choose the moment with care, and you light up when it comes. It isn't a no that you dread. It's a flat "just tell me" from someone who's stopped playing along, or the day your little delays become what everyone expects. And there's one seat in the game you never take: the one where you're the one waiting.

You give people something to look forward to. With you, an ordinary evening gets a reason to linger, and a tease is an invitation into the game.

**yours**

1. In nineteenth-century France, cafés served a plain little drink: coffee and a spirit, simply mixed. New Orleans took that café drink and turned it into Café Brûlot, a coffee prepared at the table over several careful steps. It's said Jules Alciatore first made it at Antoine's, the restaurant his father founded, which still serves on St Louis Street. Galatoire's and Commander's Palace make it too, and to many people it's part of eating in New Orleans.

2. One classic recipe soaks cinnamon and peels of lemon and orange for hours in cognac and kirsch, a clear cherry brandy. Then the warm brandy runs down a long spiral of orange peel studded with cloves. Only then, in the classic recipe, comes the coffee, the very thing everyone ordered, and pouring it in puts out the brandy's flame.

3. Nobody is fooled. Everyone there knows the coffee is coming. And I like to think the person carrying it out enjoys every face while choosing the moment. That's you, teasing, exactly. Coffee after dinner is about the most ordinary thing there is, and New Orleans gave it a build-up. You do that to an ordinary evening.

4. The cocktail I've made for you follows the classic recipe's order, in my own measures, for two little coffee cups, and it's never lit. Cognac and kirsch sit for a few hours with the peels and cinnamon. Then they're warmed gently with syrup made from demerara sugar, and run down a clove-studded orange spiral into the cups. It's warm, dark and spiced, with the cherry as the surprise. The coffee, made with chicory the New Orleans way, comes in at the end. And one more change, just for you: someone else pours the coffee, whenever they choose.

5. So, one evening soon, let someone else decide when. Let them keep their news until the plates are cleared, or hand you the present after the decoy. Sit in their seat for once and enjoy not knowing. You'll feel what you've been giving people all along, and you'll find the game is even better with two. I hope someone keeps you guessing.

# Pour — The Kind You'd Want · The Elf/Imp (jester-magician)

## Cocktail

- **name:** The Kind You'd Want
- **tagline:** Your mischief makes grown-ups feel like they're allowed to play.
- **glassware:** a plain everyday tumbler (about 300 ml), filled with ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 45 ml | apple brandy, oak-aged (a Calvados, or an American straight apple brandy, not applejack, 40-50%) | from the bottle in the fridge |
| 20 ml | dry vermouth | from the bottle; kept cold and undiluted, it lasts longer |
| 5 ml | rich syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight) | from the bottle |
| 110 ml | soda water, cold | added in the glass, never in the bottle |
| 1 strip | lemon peel, no white pith | squeezed over the top, then dropped in |

**method**
1. Make the rich syrup: warm 200 g sugar with 100 g water, stirring, until it's clear. Let it cool.
2. Make the bottle (six drinks): pour 270 ml apple brandy, 120 ml dry vermouth and 30 ml rich syrup into a clean 500 ml bottle. Close it and turn it over a few times. No water and no soda go in the bottle: vermouth in a watered-down cocktail changes within a few hours.
3. Label the bottle: the drink's name, "apple brandy, strong", and "70 ml over ice, top with soda". Keep it in the fridge. Use it within about a month; it's at its best while the bottle is still full.
4. To serve, fill a plain tumbler with ice and pour in 70 ml from the bottle.
5. Top with 110 ml cold soda water (130 ml if your apple brandy is stronger than 50%) and stir once, gently.
6. Squeeze a strip of lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Label the bottle before it goes in the fridge. Then plant your next surprise somewhere it's still going once you've left the house.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Poured from a bottle in the fridge, like anything else. It isn't anything else.*

**whoYouAre**
Somebody's keys are in the fruit bowl, under the bananas, and you're helping them look, very seriously. This morning every mug in the cupboard was turned to face the wall. They call it trouble, and they keep letting you in anyway.

Nobody spots the rules. Every trick fits one person, and everything can be put right in seconds. The mugs go back. The keys turn up before anyone's late. For every trick people see, there are a few you decided against, because of who'd be on the end of it. What you're afraid of is the trick that lands wrong and becomes somebody's bad day. So you keep them small, and gone by teatime.

You make a house a place where being surprised is safe, and around you, grown-ups still get to play.

**yours**

1. In the 2000s, Brian Shebairo owned a rough-and-tumble hot-dog shop on St. Mark's Place in New York, and was turning the bubble-tea lounge next door into a bar. His first plan was a rock-and-roll bar. It became a cocktail bar instead, and the door to it was his idea: a phone booth, at the back of the hot-dog shop. "A little Get Smart," he called it, after the 1960s TV spy spoof whose hero steps into a phone booth and dials a number.

2. The bar opened in 2007. More than a decade later, that phone booth was still its door, and one writer calls it, with a careful "arguably", the most famous bar entrance in the world. It's the same bar as another of my stories, but that one belongs to someone else.

3. I like to think that's exactly the joke you'd make, and exactly how you'd make it: played completely straight. No wink, just a phone booth in a hot-dog shop, where a phone booth has every right to be. Nobody gets hurt. The worst that can happen is you open a door and find a bar. But there's one difference from yours. His wasn't put back by teatime. It stayed. And I like to think it went on catching somebody new on a quiet weeknight, years after he first thought of it, without him there to watch it land.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is built on the same joke. It's a highball: apple brandy, dry vermouth and a spoon of rich syrup, mixed in a bottle that waits, labelled, in the fridge. Whenever someone wants one, they pour a little over ice in a plain tumbler, top it up with cold soda water, then squeeze a lemon peel over it. It looks like any fizzy thing you'd find in a fridge. It tastes like a proper cocktail: dry and bright, apple first, with lemon over the top. Nothing in it is hidden, and the label says what it is. The only trick is that it's there, ready, long after whoever made it has gone out, as a nod to a phone booth that kept being a door.

5. Keep your rules. They're why people let you in. But make one that stays. Not a trick for this afternoon: a surprise built into something that lasts. A note in the pocket of a coat they won't wear until winter. A line written inside a book you lend. You won't be there when it lands, and that's the point. Months from now someone will find it, grin at nobody, and know exactly who it was.

- **tagline:** Your straight face brings out everyone else's funniest side.
- **glassware:** large plain tumbler (about 350 ml), three ice cubes

**method**
1. Squeeze half a lime into a large tumbler, then drop the squeezed half in after the juice.
2. Add three ice cubes, then the rye.
3. Top up with the cold mineral water, poured gently so it keeps its bubbles. Stir once.
4. No sugar, and nothing on top.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Named after a regular, mixed by the bartender. The regular denied being its author.*

**whoYouAre**
Everyone around you thinks the funny one is your friend: the one who waves both arms through every story, gets the order wrong on purpose and starts the singing. You're sitting beside them, saying very little. You let them run, then one quiet word, or just a look, and the whole table goes. They get the laugh. It comes off you. Most of them take you for the serious one, and you go along with it, since that's part of the act.

How much you're enjoying it is the bit you hide best. You'd never say it, but you need them to be ridiculous. Put you in a room where everyone behaves and you're bored within the hour. People think you put up with the loudest person at the table. You picked them. Your fear is being taken at face value, as the grown-up who doesn't get the joke. You get it before anyone. And that's a gift to everyone near you: next to you, they're at their funniest, because someone steady is there to play it against.

**yours**

1. By the end of 1889, at a Washington bar everyone called Shoo's, a new drink had caught on: whiskey, half a lime, soda water and ice, and no sugar at all. It carried the name of a regular, a lobbyist known as Colonel Joe Rickey, who, it's said, showed bartenders how to make it wherever he went. Mixing it was the head bartender, George Williamson, who worked there for years and stayed with the drink a long time.

2. Then the comedy starts. In 1893 Rickey told a New York paper that he wasn't the drink's author at all, and at least three of his own accounts of how it began were printed in his lifetime. A later writer named Williamson as the real inventor. Even the lime has its stories: in Rickey's own, the switch to lime came from one of the bartenders; in another, a stranger handed Williamson the limes. Whether or not Rickey drank it himself, his friends did, and ordered it by his name. And in 1895, when he wrote his recipe out by hand for a newspaper, the lime was in it.

3. George Williamson, I like to think, loved it, and heard each new version of how the drink started, said nothing, and poured it again. The colonel had the name and the stories. The bartender had the drink. It doesn't work without both of them, and the steady one knows that better than anyone. So do you. You don't want the name on it. You want the act to work, and the act works because of you.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Rickey, a renowned classic, made with whiskey, the way it caught on at Shoo's: long, very cold and bone dry. Each partner puts something in. From the bar, a straight rye, because Shoo's sold its own and it often went into this drink. From the colonel, his water: he reportedly preferred Apollinaris, a sparkling mineral water, and I like to think it makes the lime taste a little brighter. The half lime belongs to both of them, whoever started it. The water is there as a nod to him, and the rye to the bar where Williamson poured, because I couldn't make it with only one of them.

5. You give everyone their best moment, and the one person nobody's watching is you. Once in a while, let it show. Let the loudest person at the table see you laugh. They've been playing to you from the start, and your laugh is the one they wanted most. The act survives it. They'll know you were having fun all along, and you get to have it with them, out in the open.

# Pour — Hoping You'd Come · The Geisha (lover-caregiver)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Hoping You'd Come
- **tagline:** You make room for people before you ask them to come.
- **glassware:** a small wineglass (about 250 ml), one plain lump of ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| about 60 g | roasted apple (roughly half a medium apple, peeled and cored) | wrapped in wet brown paper and roasted until soft, as Willard's recipe has it. Then left to cool. |
| 60 ml | brandy (grape brandy: a VSOP cognac, or any aged grape brandy of about 40%) | the captain's page says only "brandy"; Wondrich reads it as the grape brandy he preferred |
| 60 ml | cold water | |
| 1½ tsp (about 6 g) | sugar | Willard used as much sugar as brandy; I cut it to a teaspoon and a half, or it would be more than four times too sweet |
| 1 | lump of ice | ordinary ice, one piece |

**method**
1. An hour or more before anyone comes, peel and core the apples, half an apple for each drink. Wet a sheet of brown paper (a brown paper bag soaked under the tap works), wrap each apple in it, and roast at 180°C (350°F) for 30 to 45 minutes, until the apples are completely soft. Willard buried his in the embers of a fire. Let them cool.
2. Put half a roasted apple and the sugar in the glass, and mash them together with a spoon.
3. Add the brandy and the cold water, and stir until the sugar has gone and the apple is loose in the drink. Do this before anyone arrives, in the glass or in a jug for several. It will wait.
4. When they come, give it a stir, add one lump of ice, stir a few more turns, and serve with the spoon in the glass.

**closingLine:** *Roast the apples. While they cool, call the one you'd most like to see.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A captain wrote this toddy down from a barman who, people said, never forgot a face.*

**whoYouAre**
Someone's coming over. Long before they get there, you've been at it: the chair moved nearer the heater for the one who always feels the cold, the music down to where people can talk, the light just so. By the time they walk in, it looks as if it all happened by itself. That's the idea. Nobody should feel they put you to any trouble. They should just feel expected.

What you'd never tell them is: I was hoping you'd come. All that getting ready is how you hope without asking. A room made ready can't be turned down, and a plain question can. The thought you don't let yourself stay with is the ready room with nobody in it. People leave your evenings with the feeling that someone had them in mind before they arrived, even when they couldn't say why.

**yours**

1. In New York, back when hotel guests checked in at the bar, the City Hotel's desk clerk and its bartender were the same man, Orsamus Willard. People told a story about him. A guest sailed to England, stayed ten years, and walked back into the bar. Willard greeted him by name, and remembered his old room number.

2. They said he almost never left the hotel, and that he'd do anything he could to make a guest comfortable. He left no book and no account of his own life, and even the plain facts of it are hard to find. When he went home to Massachusetts, his house had a number on every room door. I like to think he was still getting rooms ready, for guests who might or might not come.

3. That's where I see you in him. Not the famous memory. The rooms made ready anyway.

4. One of his guests did write his toddy down. A British army captain who drank at his bar printed a few recipes in his travel book, and credited one of them to Willard by name: the Apple Toddy, one of the renowned drinks that made the American bar famous abroad. After Prohibition, it all but disappeared. The cocktail I've made for you is made after Willard's: the best apples rolled in wet paper and roasted until soft, then equal measures of apple, brandy and water, as he had them, and one lump of ice. His called for as much sugar as brandy, far too sweet by today's taste, so I kept it to a teaspoon and a half. For the brandy, I took the grape brandy the historian David Wondrich believes Willard preferred. Nearly all of it happens before anyone arrives: the apples roast, cool and wait. I kept it that way as a nod to you, because that's where your care always starts.

5. So next time you're getting a room ready, add the one thing you always leave out. Ask. Not "come by sometime": the plain sentence, to the person you're hoping will come. Getting ready is how you hope. Asking is how they find out they were hoped for. And I wish you a full house.

In November 1889, a reporter called Nellie Bly set out to go round the world faster than the hero of Jules Verne's novel, who took eighty days. She had promised seventy-five. # Pour — Only Half Joking · The Flirt (lover-jester)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Only Half Joking
- **tagline:** Every tease is a compliment. The fun is seeing who catches it.
- **glassware:** cocktail glass (about 180-200 ml), chilled
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 45 ml | London dry gin | any London dry, 37.5% or stronger |
| 22.5 ml | fresh lemon juice | squeezed today |
| 7.5 ml | Cointreau | as the recipe prints it; or any clear orange liqueur (triple sec) at 40% |
| 7.5 ml | Campari | as the recipe prints it; it brings the pink and the bitter |
| 12.5 ml | jasmine tea syrup | homemade: plain jasmine green tea and sugar, equal weights (see Method) |
| 1 | lemon peel | a wide strip, for the top |

**method**
1. Make the syrup first (it keeps about a week in the fridge): pour 100 ml of water just off the boil over 2 teaspoons (about 5 g) of plain jasmine green tea, leave it 3 minutes, strain, and stir in 100 g of white sugar until it dissolves. Let it cool.
2. Put a cocktail glass in the freezer.
3. Measure the gin, lemon, Cointreau, Campari and 2½ teaspoons (12.5 ml) of the jasmine syrup into a shaker.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Named for a friend, with one letter too many. This glass finally has jasmine in it.*

**whoYouAre**
You don't tell people you like them. You tell them their coffee order is a cry for help, that they've clearly been practising that walk, that you'll allow the hat, just this once. Then you watch. If they grin and send one back, something starts between the two of you that nobody nearby can quite follow.

Every one of those was a compliment. You just couldn't hand it over plain, because plain is too easy to turn down. Said as a joke, a no costs nobody anything, you included. What stays with you is the one who takes it at face value and looks a little hurt, or smiles politely and lets it drop, and the joke left hanging with only you holding it. And being teased by you feels like being picked. People walk away from you funnier and better-looking than they came in.

**yours**

1. At a bar called the Townhouse, in Emeryville near Oakland, a friend asked the bartender, Paul Harrington, for a drink Harrington had never made before. He says he gave it twenty seconds' thought. He took a classic he loved, put Campari in place of its bitters and lemon in place of its lime, made it once, and handed it over. In his words, it was a beautiful pink.

2. One of the first people to taste it told him he'd just invented grapefruit juice. The praise came first, then the joke. I like to think that's the whole trick, and it's your trick too: the compliment, sent sideways, to see if it's caught. Harrington also did the thing you find hardest. He said it outright, with no joke around it: he named the drink after his friend, Matt Jasmin.

3. And Harrington got it slightly wrong. Years later he realised he'd been spelling the name with an "e" on the end, a letter Matt's name doesn't have. By then, it was too late. His 1998 book carried the drink to bartenders around the world, and it went on to be called a modern classic, extra letter and all. I recognise you in that: when you finally say the nice thing out loud, you're sure it'll come out a little wrong. His did. It still carries his friend's name, near enough.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is built on that Jasmine. It's gin and squeezed lemon with small measures of Cointreau and Campari, shaken hard and poured very cold into a frosted stemmed glass, with the oils of a lemon peel misted across it. All of Harrington's measures are there. My one addition is a little syrup made from jasmine tea. That extra "e" spells his friend's name the way English spells the flower, and the recipe Harrington printed has no jasmine in it. I've put some in, years late, as my tease played back to him. The syrup softens the tartness, so it ends up bright, a little bitter and softly scented.

5. Next time someone plays back, don't send another tease. Tell them what the last one was hiding: that they're funny, that they're good company, that the hat is actually great. Once, plainly. It may come out clumsy. Harrington's came out with a letter too many, and it stuck. Plenty of people you like have no idea how much, and the ones you tell will play back hardest of all.

| amount | item | note |
