# Pour — Who's In? · The Charismatic Leader (ruler-jester)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Who's In?
- **tagline:** People follow your lead because it feels like joining the fun.
- **glassware:** a big glass (about 400 ml, a 14-oz highball or double old-fashioned), chilled in the freezer, packed with crushed ice and a straw
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | vodka | any unflavoured vodka from 37.5% to 45% |
| 20 ml | fresh lime juice | |
| 15 ml (1 tbsp) | raspberry and toasted cumin syrup | homemade: fresh raspberries, the same weight of sugar and a little toasted cumin, blended cold and sieved. Keeps a week in the fridge |
| 6 | fresh mint leaves | they stay in the glass |
| one of | 3 or 4 more mint leaves, or ½ tsp (2.5 ml) more syrup, or 1 dash Angostura bitters | your call, after you've tasted it through the straw |
| to fill | crushed ice | lots of it: more ice than drink |
| garnish | a mint sprig and two fresh raspberries | on top of the ice |

**method**
1. Make the syrup ahead. Warm half a teaspoon of cumin seeds in a dry frying pan, shaking it, until they smell nutty, then crush them lightly with the back of a spoon. Blend them cold with 100 g fresh raspberries and 100 g white sugar until the sugar has gone. Leave it for 30 minutes, then press it through a fine sieve to take out all the seeds. Keep it in the fridge.
2. Put the glass in the freezer for a few minutes.
3. Put the vodka, lime juice, syrup and mint leaves into a shaker with just a few pieces of crushed ice. Shake for about five seconds, only enough to mix it. The ice in the glass does the rest.
4. Pour everything, leaves and all, into the cold glass. Fill it four-fifths with crushed ice and stir up and down with a long spoon for a few seconds. Then pack in more ice, piled up above the rim.
5. Put a straw in and taste it. Then make one call: a few more mint leaves pushed down if you want it fresher, half a teaspoon more syrup if it's sharp, or a dash of Angostura if you want it deeper. Stir once more.
6. Top with the mint sprig and two raspberries.

**closingLine:** *Taste it through the straw and make one call. Then pass the glass to whoever hasn't made a call yet.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A bartending school went bust. Its party bar didn't. This drink comes in its big glass.*

**whoYouAre**
The last train's cancelled, and there are twelve of you on a cold platform. Someone sighs. You make a joke, it lands, and somewhere in the middle of it there's a plan, and everyone hears it: the café that's still open, the walk across town, a bet on who gets home first. Years later, it's the night everyone brings up.

Nobody calls it being in charge, because to them it feels like being asked along. You like it like that. Being obeyed bores you, and it would turn you into the boss. You seldom admit how much you enjoy having your hand on the wheel, and that when you make that first joke, you don't yet know it'll work. What you dread is the night it gets away from you, or the night the fun runs out and you're just someone telling people where to go. Around you, a plan falling apart is where the good part begins. People go further than they ever would on their own, and they come back glad they went.

**yours**

1. Six hundred pounds bought you three weeks at the London Academy of Bartenders. It opened in 1996, and it never had enough money. One of its founders, Alex Turner, said they were always one student short of being able to run the next course, so the founders worked bar jobs at night and taught in the mornings. Eventually the school went bust.

2. The name didn't. Douglas Ankrah and Richard Hargroves had a bar called LAB as well, meant, by one account, as a living advertisement for the school. The school didn't survive. The bar did, and it was never a quiet advert. Its owners wanted a party bar, loud and busy every night. Ankrah said other bars were "very, very passively boring". Jamie Terrell, whom Ankrah brought in, remembered what they were after in all that noise: "the best drinks in the world". The two of them wrote five cocktail menus together, with two hundred drinks on each.

3. It could have gone quiet. Early in 1999 it was slow, and hardly anyone noticed the place until good press turned it. After that, one bartender said everybody in the trade used to be there, to hire, to get hired, or to meet the drinks firms' reps, and it helped make bartenders into names people knew. Someone who saw it remembered the bartenders sipping a drink through a straw, then adding "a bit more mint, a little more sugar, a dash of bitters". My favourite detail: in a room that loud, someone was still tasting. I like to think you'd have got on with them. When a plan falls through, you don't mourn it. You throw the party, and you mean the party to get somewhere.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a vodka Daiquiri, built like a Mojito, in the kind of big glass LAB served so many of its drinks in, with crushed ice heaped above the rim. I chose raspberries for it, blended cold into a syrup, so the bold red comes from the fruit alone, with a pinch of toasted cumin in the syrup, a turn you won't see coming that works out, and lime and mint leaves that stay in: bright and generous. Then it's over to you. When you make it, taste it through the straw and make one of those three calls: a few more mint leaves, a little more syrup, or a dash of bitters. That step is there as a nod to those bartenders tasting in all that noise, and the drink is built so that whichever call you make, it holds.

5. Somewhere near you is someone who never makes the first joke, because you always do. When the evening next falls apart, wait a moment. Leave it to them, and follow wherever it goes. You won't lose the wheel. What you'll get is something you almost never have: the fun of not knowing where you're going while someone else steers.

## Cocktail

- **name:** Up Close
- **tagline:** People remember how you made them feel because you remember who they are.
- **glassware:** stemmed cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 small square (about 2.5 cm, 15 g) | fresh ripe pineapple | cut from near the base, where it's sweetest; no bigger, or the drink turns sharp |
| ½ tsp (2.5 ml) | rich sugar syrup | 2 parts sugar to 1 part water, stirred until clear |
| 60 ml | straight rye whiskey | any straight rye, 40% or stronger; the numbers were run on 50% |
| 20 ml | sweet vermouth | a red Italian-style vermouth |
| 2 dashes | Angostura bitters | or any aromatic bitters |
| 1 | strip of lemon peel | squeezed over the top, then dropped in |

**method**
1. Put the cocktail glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
2. Put the pineapple and the syrup in a mixing glass or jar. Press the pineapple with a muddler or the end of a rolling pin until its juice runs.
3. Add the rye, the vermouth and the bitters. Fill the mixing glass with ice.
4. Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
5. Empty the cocktail glass. Strain the drink into it through a small tea strainer, so no pineapple gets through.
6. Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Strain the pineapple out. It's still there at the rim. So are you, even when you're not trying.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A Monte Carlo barman kept his Manhattans plain. This one borrows from a regular's cocktail.*

**whoYouAre**
Someone comes back after a year away, and you ask about the interview they were dreading. You remember their sister's name. You stay with them a second longer than they expect. They go home feeling remembered.

You know exactly what your attention does, and you give it on purpose, because a lot holds together when you do. People who watch from further off call it charm, and sometimes mean it as a warning. They've got it backwards: it works because you mean it. You hardly mention what it costs, or the question underneath: if I stopped, would they still come? The fear is the evening it doesn't land, when someone looks past you and everything quietly drifts. People leave feeling they were the one who mattered, and sure enough to offer something of their own. On an ordinary evening, nobody expects to be given that.

**yours**

1. In about 1885, a sea captain's son from near Naples was made head bartender of a small bar facing the casino in Monte Carlo. Ciro Capozzi had actually tended bar in America, and where other bars poured inventions called things like Flip Flaps, he served far simpler drinks, the Manhattan among them.

2. His own bar opened in 1888, just off the casino square, and among its regulars was the Prince of Wales, who would show him cocktails he had learned. He liked American drinks already, so Ciro never had to win him over. He kept coming back, with what he knew. I like to think Ciro treasured that: the most watched man in Monte Carlo, at ease enough to teach the barman.

3. People look for the trick in you, and there isn't one. The plainness is the point: someone paying real attention, and meaning it. And the best of it was never that people are charmed. It's what they bring you once they feel seen. Anyone can be charming for an evening. You remember, you return to it, and so people offer you their best.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a Manhattan, the renowned classic Ciro was pouring in Monte Carlo. Mine is rye, sweet vermouth and bitters, stirred until ice-cold, then brightened with lemon peel. To it I've added a small square of fresh pineapple, from a cocktail of that regular's own, as a London paper had it in 1887. I like to think his own was among the ones he showed Ciro. Back then a pineapple was hugely expensive, and his drink showed it off. In this glass it goes quiet: pressed with a touch of syrup, then strained out again, as a nod to what a regular brings to the bar. It still looks like a plain Manhattan. You only find the pineapple up close.

5. Soon, for once, don't be "on". Let someone else carry the conversation, and let them show you something they've learned. Then you'll see whether they'd still come, and I hope the answer surprises you, in the best way.

# Pour — Had to Be Serious · The Revolutionary (ruler-outlaw)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Had to Be Serious
- **tagline:** You didn't just tear it down. You stayed to run it.
- **glassware:** Collins glass, filled with ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | Pimm's No. 1 Cup, recommended, or any gin-based fruit cup of about 25% | The cup the template was built on. |
| 1 tsp (5 ml) | Peychaud's bitters, recommended, or a bright-red aromatic bitters | The bitters the next book swapped in for the Pimm's. Here they go in beside it. |
| 15 ml | fresh lemon juice | |
| 2 | fresh strawberries, hulled | Muddled. |
| 3 thin slices | cucumber, plus 1 to garnish | Muddled. |
| 90 ml | soda water | To top. |
| 1 sprig | fresh mint | Clapped once, to garnish. |

**method**
1. Put the strawberries and cucumber slices in the bottom of the Collins glass with the lemon juice, and press them with a muddler until the strawberries are pulp.
2. Add the Pimm's, then spoon in the Peychaud's.
3. Fill the glass with ice, top with the soda water, and stir gently, lifting the fruit up from the bottom.
4. Lay the mint sprig on one palm and clap your hands together once, just hard enough to release its smell without tearing it. Set it in the glass beside a cucumber slice.

**closingLine:** *Spoon the bitters in before the soda. When the next one comes, ask what they'd put in its place.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*In one rebel drink, these bitters replaced the Pimm's. In this glass, they share it.*

**whoYouAre**
You were the one who said the old way was finished. People laughed. Then they let you try, it worked, and the new way was yours to keep going: the rota, the budget, the wet Tuesday when nobody remembers why anything changed. Most people who start a fight are gone by then. You stayed.

You'd rarely admit it, but you never wanted a free-for-all. You wanted it run properly, by you, and you had the plan for afterwards before the argument was over. The day you dread is someone new standing where you stood, saying what you said, and you hearing yourself answer the way they once answered you. But staying is the hard part, and hardly anyone thanks you for it. You make the better way real, and keep it real, so the people who wanted it actually get to live in it.

**yours**

1. Toby Maloney came from the club world, where he could turn out seven vodka drinks in fifteen seconds. A tiny New York bar where one round took fifteen minutes struck him as laughable. He took a night a week behind its bar anyway, thinking he might learn something.

2. In 2007, The Violet Hour opened with him behind the bar, in Chicago, then mostly a city of beer and whiskey. Later, one bartender said the city's bartending family trees ran back to two people, and he was one.

3. He has since said he cringes at some of it, like refusing to make a vodka Martini because he thought it was beneath him. He also said he doesn't think any of this would exist without that seriousness. He kept both halves. A few years on, one of his protégés co-wrote a small book of radical recipes, a reaction, his co-author said, to how boring a lot of cocktail people were. Maloney contributed to it.

4. That's you in one life: the newcomer who laughed, the strict one who held the line, the old hand who gave something to whoever came next. You know the cringe at how hard you once had to push, and you'd still never say it was wrong to push. And one day, years in, someone younger looks at what you built the way you once looked at the old way.

5. The cocktail I've made for you starts from the Pimm's Cup that one of that book's recipes began with, a British summer cooler: muddled strawberry and cucumber, the Pimm's left in, a little lemon, and soda. Then one spoonful of the bright red bitters their book swapped in for the Pimm's. The measures, the lemon and one more touch are my own: a sprig of mint, clapped once between the palms, a trick Maloney pioneered, as a nod to what you bring to whatever the next one makes. Your order is still the glass. Their change is in it.

6. When someone you've taught comes back and tells you it's all got a bit boring, don't defend it first. Ask what they'd do instead, and give them something towards it. You had your answer ready once. So might they, and whatever they build will carry some of you in it.

# Pour — One Table · The People's Representative (ruler-regular-guy)

## Cocktail

- **name:** One Table
- **tagline:** You give both sides a place at a table they thought they couldn't share.
- **glassware:** large rocks glass (about 300 ml), one large ice cube
- **contains:** `["nuts"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 ml | straight rye whiskey | 40% or stronger; a 50% bottled-in-bond rye is what the numbers were run on |
| 30 ml | cognac | any VS or VSOP cognac, 40% or stronger |
| 30 ml | sweet vermouth steeped with cardamom | made the night before (see Method); start from any Italian-style sweet vermouth, as the 1937 recipe asks |
| 1 tsp (5 ml) | Bénédictine D.O.M. | recommended, as the old recipe names it; or a honeyed French herbal liqueur. Bénédictine contains nutmeg: check any substitute's label for nuts |
| 2 dashes | Peychaud's bitters | recommended, as the old recipe names it; or any New Orleans-style aromatic bitters |
| 2 dashes | Angostura bitters | or any aromatic bitters |
| 1 | strip of lemon peel | squeezed over the top, then dropped in |

**method**
1. The night before, put about 3 g of whole green cardamom pods (roughly 15) into 250 ml of sweet vermouth in a clean jar. Leave it at room temperature for about 12 hours, then strain it back into its bottle and keep it in the fridge. It's enough for eight drinks.
2. Pour the rye and the cognac into a mixing glass or jar, just as they come from the bottle.
3. Add the cardamom vermouth, the Bénédictine and both bitters. Fill the mixing glass with ice.
4. Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
5. Put one large ice cube in the rocks glass and strain the drink over it.
6. Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Put the cardamom in the vermouth, never in either spirit. Next time you cross over, bring all of yourself.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A city gave up brandy for whiskey. Years later, one glass poured both.*

**whoYouAre**
A family stops speaking over a seating plan. A team splits down the middle over who did the work. Two neighbours each want you to say the other one's wrong. Everyone waits to see which table you'll sit at. You go and sit with the people who expected you not to, and you have whatever they're having.

You don't do it with a speech. You've never won anyone round with an argument, and you don't try. You just turn up on their ground and mean it. From outside it can look like sitting on the fence. It isn't. You have a side, and you know your own mind. The hardest question you get doesn't come from the other side. It comes from your own: whose side are you on? What you fear is being made to choose, and the day a row stops being a row and becomes the way things are. Because of you, nobody has to pick a table. Both halves end up in one room, and neither had to give itself up to get there.

**yours**

1. Before the American Civil War, New Orleans was a brandy town. Its juleps were made with brandy, and that was how the city drank. Then the city changed. By 1885, a bartender was telling a New Orleans newspaper that brandy drinking there was over, and that whiskey had taken its place. The city drank it in whiskey cocktails and in the new Manhattan.

2. By the 1930s, the Hotel Monteleone's head bartender was Walter Bergeron. He'd worked that bar before Prohibition and returned when it ended. The drink he created there became the hotel's signature. It's a Manhattan at heart, but where a Manhattan has whiskey, his has two spirits: rye whiskey and French cognac. They go in at equal measures, level with the sweet vermouth, plus two different bitters and a touch of a herbal liqueur from France, Bénédictine. Its name is the old quarter's: Vieux Carré, "old square".

3. He said he made it to honour the old quarter. Why he put those two spirits side by side, he didn't say. But I like to think it's the city's whole story in a single drink: the brandy it drank first and the whiskey it turned to, together in one glass, neither poured a drop less than the other. That's what you do. When people split, you don't rule on which half was right. You bring both in, at the same weight, and you call it by a name everyone already shares.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is the Vieux Carré, a renowned New Orleans classic, with the proportions of its first printed recipe: rye, cognac and sweet vermouth in three equal measures, none cut back for another. I didn't change either spirit. I steeped the vermouth overnight with green cardamom, as a nod to the ground the two sides share: of the three measures, the vermouth is the one that belongs to neither, and cardamom goes with both the grain behind the rye and the grape behind the cognac. It's stirred, rich and deep, with the rye's spice and the cognac's softer fruit each as clear as the other, and the cardamom warm in the vermouth between them.

5. When you go over to the other side, you tend to leave a little of yourself at the door, so they feel safe. Your own side notices, and that's where the question comes from. Don't pour less of yourself. It was never your quietness they trusted. It's that you came as you are and stayed. And when your own side asks again, you'll have your answer: both, and still me.

**closing line (Tomás, r4):** *Put the cardamom in the vermouth, never in either spirit. Next time you cross over, bring all of yourself.*

# Pour — Either Way · The Judge (ruler-sage)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Either Way
- **tagline:** You want a fair answer, even when it means changing your mind.
- **glassware:** old-fashioned glass (rocks glass, about 300 ml), filled with ice cubes
- **contains:** `["gluten"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | blended Scotch whisky | any blend, 40-43%: malt and grain whisky together |
| 7.5 ml (1½ tsp) | malt syrup | 1 part barley malt syrup (from a jar, the baking shelf) to 2 parts rich sugar syrup, stirred smooth; up to 1¾ tsp if your malt syrup is dark |
| 2 dashes | aromatic bitters (Angostura) | |
| 1 | orange peel strip | squeezed over the top, then dropped in |

**method**
1. Make the malt syrup: stir 1 tablespoon of barley malt syrup into 2 tablespoons of rich sugar syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water by weight, dissolved warm) until no streaks are left. It keeps in the fridge for weeks.
2. Put the malt syrup and the bitters in the glass, add the whisky, and stir to mix.
3. Fill the glass with ice cubes and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass is cold.
4. Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *Stir until you can't see the malt. Then say what you've decided, and let the argument go on without you.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*There's whisky in this glass that rival distillers once insisted wasn't whisky at all.*

**whoYouAre**
Two friends fall out, and sooner or later each of them tells you their side. You hear both out to the end, and you ask for the bits that don't flatter them. Then you tell them plainly what you think happened, and it's rarely what either of them hoped. When trouble comes round again, it's the one you disagreed with who calls first.

People assume plain speaking is easy for you. It isn't, not once. You want to be liked as much as anyone, and later, alone, you replay the conversation, half hoping someone will show you what you missed. What you won't put up with is the kind-sounding fudge, the "let's not make a fuss", because you know who pays for it, and it's never the person saying it. It's the quietest one there. With you, the quietest voice gets the same answer as the loudest, and it matters more than they ever tell you.

**yours**

1. For decades, distillers argued about a word. In the 1830s, whisky makers in the Lowlands took up a new kind of still, one that could run without stopping, and made a light, pure grain whisky cheap enough for city factory workers. The makers of malt whisky, from the old pot stills, said the new spirit wasn't whisky at all. They had age and tradition on their side. The grain side had the size: in 1877, six of the biggest grain distillers joined forces.

2. In 1908 a British commission sat and took evidence in person from across the spirits trade. Where it landed was plain. Whisky was a spirit distilled from cereal grain, its starch turned to sugar by malt, and nothing in that said which still. The new spirit was whisky. Blending stayed legal, and the commission set out what a label could claim.

3. That settled the law, not the argument. Over decades of marketing, the idea that the older whisky is the real one has largely won people over. The ruling stood anyway. That will be familiar to you: a call that went against the side with age and tradition, and then held, liked or not. I like to think the people it looked after most weren't in the room at all: whoever was buying the cheaper bottle.

4. The cocktail I've made for you starts from one of the most renowned classics of all, the Old-Fashioned. I make it with blended Scotch: malt and grain whisky together, the two whiskies that argument was about. Only the sugar is different. I sweeten it with a syrup made partly from barley malt, which the commission's definition asked of every whisky, whatever still it came from. That's as a nod to how you treat people: one rule, whichever side they're on. The malt makes it rounder and warmer than plain sugar would. Angostura goes in as well, the glass is a heavy one packed with ice, and last, orange peel is squeezed above it for its scent.

5. Once everyone's been heard and you've made the call, you've done the fair part. You don't also owe the room its agreement. Some of them will never come round, and that doesn't make the call any less fair. If the evidence ever changes, it'll find you, because you're the one who always asks for it. Until then, take the evening off from deciding. You've earned the nights when nobody needs an answer from you.

# Pour — Further Than Me · The Mentor (sage-caregiver)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Further Than Me
- **tagline:** You teach people to trust their own judgement, even when it takes them beyond yours.
- **glassware:** highball glass, chilled, filled with ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | London dry gin | ideally 43% or stronger; 40% works, just a touch lighter |
| 30 ml | fresh lemon juice | lemon, as Oxford's Southside has it |
| 22.5 ml | simple syrup | equal weights of sugar and water, stirred until clear |
| 6 | fresh mint leaves | shaken in and strained out |
| 8 | fresh tarragon leaves | about the tip of one sprig; shaken in beside the mint, strained out |
| 60 ml | soda water, cold | added last |
| 1 + 1 | sprig of mint and sprig of tarragon | to finish, set in together |

**method**
1. Put the highball glass in the freezer for ten minutes, then fill it with ice.
2. Put the gin, lemon juice, simple syrup, mint leaves and tarragon leaves in a shaker. Fill it with ice and shake hard but briefly, about five seconds, so there's room left for the soda.
3. Pour it through the shaker's strainer and a small tea strainer into the glass, so no bits of leaf get through.
4. Add the cold soda water and give it one quick stir.
5. Clap the mint sprig and the tarragon sprig once between your hands to wake their scent, then set them in the glass together.

**closingLine:** *Put the two sprigs in together. Then find out what one of them knows now that you don't.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*The 21 Club's house drink for many years. The second herb in it is mine.*

**whoYouAre**
Someone rings with a decision they can't make and asks what you'd do. You could tell them. Usually you don't, at least not at first. You ask what they've noticed so far, you say what you'd keep an eye on, and you let them get to the end of the sentence themselves. It takes longer. The one thing you couldn't live with is someone following you into a wrong answer. What they work out for themselves is theirs, to keep or to change.

Then one day they stop ringing. They've got it. Years later they explain something to you, faster and better than you'd have managed, and you feel two things at once: very proud, and slightly left behind. You only ever mention the first. That's better than any answer you could have handed them: they leave able to manage on their own, and sure they always could.

**yours**

1. There was a time when New York's 21 Club was arguably the best-known bar anywhere. Brian Rea was hired there, and Jerry Berns schooled him in running a bar and a restaurant. Rea was an enthusiastic student. He became head bartender. Then he left.

2. Another bar followed, then the West Coast. In 1969 he dreamed up a new job, the beverage director, who would run the bar and the drinks separately from the food. He talked to six big hospitality companies about it, and one said yes. I like to think the lessons took precisely because he carried them somewhere else: taught the bar and the restaurant as one business, he made a job out of setting them apart.

3. Berns lived until 2006, so that new job came well within his lifetime. We don't know if Berns followed it. I like to think he did, and that he was glad the idea wasn't his. That's what I recognise in you. You've never wanted anyone to turn into a copy of you. The day someone you helped goes past you is the day you know it worked.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is the Southside, a classic and, for many years, the 21 Club's house drink: gin, fresh lemon, sugar and mint, shaken, poured over ice in a chilled highball glass and lifted with soda. It's crisp and bright, the way a long drink should be. And I added one thing of my own, a few leaves of tarragon shaken in beside the mint, as a nod to the student who took what he was taught somewhere new. Tarragon shares some of what makes lemon smell of lemon, so it belongs with the rest, and still it brings something of its own. To finish, a sprig of each goes in together, both standing tall, neither one hidden behind the other.

# Pour — Look Again · The Philosopher (sage-explorer)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Look Again
- **tagline:** The more you like an answer, the harder you look at it.
- **glassware:** rocks glass (about 300 ml), filled with ice cubes
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 ml | French grape brandy | any VS cognac or Armagnac, about 40%. It goes in first |
| 45 ml | oude (old-style) genever | Dutch or Belgian: look for "oude" on the label, not "jonge" (young). "Oude" means the older, maltier style, not aged. 35% or stronger |
| 6 ml (about 1¼ tsp) | rich sugar syrup | 2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight, stirred until clear |
| 2 dashes | Angostura bitters | |
| 1 strip | lemon peel | |

**method**
1. Pour the brandy into the rocks glass first.
2. Add the syrup and the bitters, then pour the genever on top.
3. Give it a quick stir, fill the glass with ice cubes, and stir again for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
4. Squeeze the lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.

**closingLine:** *The brandy goes in before the genever. Love the next neat idea, then learn what it started as.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*"Gin" began as a short form of the name of the spirit in this glass.*

**whoYouAre**
Over dinner, a friend explains a lovely theory about how something famous really began. It's neat, it has a name and a date in it, and you love it at once. Hours later you're still in your chair, turning it over. People take that for doubt. It's closer to the reverse: you fall for ideas faster than anyone you know, which is exactly why you check the ones you love.

What worries you is your own delight: a lovely idea, passed on with confidence, that turns out to be wrong. And when a favourite doesn't survive a closer look, you let it go without a fuss. Nobody sees what that costs you.

You take other people's ideas as seriously as your own. Someone floats a half-thought, and you follow it further than they dared, and they leave feeling cleverer than they came. It's respect, and it means more to them than you know.

**yours**

1. There's a famous answer to who invented gin, repeated so widely that drinks historians despair of ever shifting it: a chemist in Holland called Sylvius. It took hold in 1824, when Samuel Morewood wrote that a German traveller, Engelbert Kämpfer, had credited the spirit's discovery to "Professor Sylvius of Leiden". Morewood was nobody's fool. He's been called the founder of the field, and his history of distilling was the first full one. He was probably right, too, that the spirit Kämpfer meant was genever, the Dutch spirit gin grew out of.

2. Maybe Sylvius did make a fine one. Kämpfer seems to have meant just that: Sylvius's own version of a spirit the Dutch were already making. Morewood read it as the invention of the spirit itself, and most of the writers who came after him took his word without question. Historians have only recently begun to correct it. Genever goes back at least to the late 1400s, more than a century before Sylvius was born, and the author of its earliest known recipe is unknown.

3. I like to think the answer lasted because it was such a good one: a name, a title, a city. It's exactly the kind of answer you'd love. And you're also the one who'd go back to the traveller's words late at night, and find the claim smaller than it looked, and the spirit under it older and bigger. I see both of those people in you: the one who loves the neat answer, and the one who goes back anyway.

4. So the cocktail I've made for you is built on the older spirit. It's that classic of classics, the Old-Fashioned, made after a New York bartender's recipe of 1895, which came in a Holland gin version too: a little sugar, Angostura, lemon peel, ice. The spirit is oude genever, the old style (the word names the style, not years in a barrel): rich, malty, closer to a whisky than to the gin you know, which took its short name from it. Under it, poured in before the genever, is a little French grape brandy, distilled from wine, as a nod to the wine Dutch distillers made their spirit from before they turned to grain. Once it's stirred you can't find the layers. The older one is in every sip.

5. So keep loving the neat answers. Don't change that. Just, next time one delights you, don't save the going back for midnight and your own chair. Go back with the friend who brought it: "I love that. Want to see what's underneath?" Most of the time, what the two of you find is older and bigger than the story you started with, and it's theirs to keep too. Going back stops being the lonely part, and becomes what the evening was for.

# Pour — At the Time · The Grandmaster (sage-hero)

## Cocktail

- **name:** At the Time
- **tagline:** You see far enough ahead to let a quick win go.
- **glassware:** heavy double old-fashioned glass (about 350 ml), one large block of coffee ice
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50 ml | barrel-proof (cask-strength) straight rye whiskey | any, 55 to 62%; if yours is 63 to 68%, use 25 ml of water below instead of 15 |
| 12.5 ml (2½ tsp) | demerara syrup | equal weights demerara sugar and hot water, stirred until dissolved, cooled |
| 2 dashes | Angostura bitters | |
| 15 ml | cold water | |
| 1 large block | coffee ice | ordinary black coffee (filter or cafetière, no sugar, no milk), brewed the way you'd drink it, cooled, then frozen overnight in a large silicone cube mould (about 5 cm) |
| 1 strip | orange peel | |

**method**
1. The day before, brew the coffee, let it cool, pour it into the mould and freeze it overnight.
2. Put the rye, syrup, bitters and water in a mixing glass or a jar, fill it with ordinary ice and stir for about 30 seconds, until it's cold and the whiskey's burn has softened but not gone.
3. Put the coffee block in the glass and strain the drink over it.
4. Squeeze the peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
5. The first sips are the Old-Fashioned alone. As the block melts, a dark layer gathers around it; give the glass a slow swirl whenever you like, and the coffee comes into the drink.

**closingLine:** *Swirl it once the coffee starts to show. When you miss one, make the next move just as steadily.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Rye, sugar, bitters, peel. The coffee is in the ice, and arrives later.*

**whoYouAre**
You turned down the offer everyone said you'd regret. Or you let the first chance go by, or gave up a point in an argument you could easily have won. People shook their heads, kindly, and it looked as if you'd got it wrong. You let it look that way. You couldn't prove it yet, and you won't promise what you can't show.

It costs you, too. Letting go of the sure thing never feels clever. It's a loss, and you carry it, saying nothing, until the move plays out. You don't mind looking as if you've got it wrong for a while. What you mind is the move you didn't see, after people trusted you to have read it all.

When everyone wants the quick win, you can sit through the slow one, and whoever is with you can stop panicking. That steadiness is a kindness, even on the days it gets called stubbornness.

**yours**

1. By the late 1990s, Cedd Moses had worn himself out at work and sold his company. He turned to property. Going out to bars and restaurants in Los Angeles had left him in love with the city's rundown old centre, which one book calls dead. He says he went downtown to open bars and bring the area and the city's cocktails back, out of pride in the city and a love for its old buildings. He started buying property there while it was cheap. "Everyone at the time thought I was insane," he remembers.

2. His first bar was Golden Gopher, but the same history says it was a later one, Seven Grand, that made the difference: mostly a whiskey bar, where a lot of promising bartenders worked. Chuck Taggart, an early cocktail lover in the city, called its opening the big turning point, "to me": it wasn't the first, he said, but it seemed to set off so many others. Moses kept opening bars after that.

3. We don't know how it felt to him while he was buying. I like to think the buying didn't feel clever then, more like a price paid early, with nothing yet to show for it and everyone shaking their heads. That's the piece of this story I'd hand you: the move made before it could be judged, the stretch of looking wrong, and a first try that came before the one that made the difference. I like the size of the ending, too. We don't know whether he ever got everything he went downtown for. The record is smaller: a history that says Seven Grand made the difference, and one man who calls it, "to me", the turning point. I suspect you trust that ending more than a triumphant one.

4. The cocktail I've made for you is a famous classic, the Old-Fashioned, built strong on a barrel-proof rye, because Seven Grand was a whiskey bar (the rye is my choice). It's sweetened with demerara, seasoned with Angostura, stirred cold, poured over one block of frozen black coffee, with the oil of an orange peel added last. Anyone who knows an Old-Fashioned may think I've got the ice wrong. The first sips are the Old-Fashioned alone, strong and good on their own. Then, as the block melts, the coffee gathers in a dark ring around it, and one slow swirl brings it in, its roast meeting the toasted side of the grain. The coffee is in the ice because of those years downtown: the move is made first, and nobody can taste it yet.

5. One day there'll be a trap you don't see. Not because you weren't paying attention: you were, more closely than anyone at the table. Some things can't be read from where anyone is sitting. When it happens, it doesn't mean the people who doubted you were right. Take that loss as plainly as you take the ones you choose, and carry on. You'll have lost a piece you didn't mean to give. You'll still have everything that made you good at this.

# Pour — In Good Part · The Wise Fool (sage-jester)

## Cocktail

- **name:** In Good Part
- **tagline:** Your jokes let people change their minds without losing face.
- **glassware:** coupe, chilled in the freezer, no ice in the glass
- **contains:** `["egg-white"]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60 ml | Plymouth gin, recommended | as Oxford's Clover Club recipe prints it; or any soft, earthy dry gin, less juniper-led than a London dry, about 41-44% |
| 15 ml | fresh lemon juice | squeezed the same day |
| 35 ml | raspberry and red wine syrup | homemade: 100 g fresh raspberries, 100 g white sugar and 100 ml dry young red wine (a Cabernet Sauvignon style), blended cold and sieved; makes about 250 ml, enough for seven drinks; keeps a week in the fridge |
| 15 ml | egg white | about half a large white, loosened with a fork first so it pours |

**Glassware:** coupe, chilled in the freezer, no ice in the glass.
**Contains:** egg-white.

**method**
1. Up to a week ahead, make the syrup. Put the raspberries, sugar and wine in a blender and blend on low until you can't feel any sugar grains, about a minute. Leave it 30 minutes, then press it through a fine sieve to take out the seeds. Jar it and keep it in the fridge.
2. Put the coupe in the freezer.
3. Crack an egg, keep the white, and whisk it lightly with a fork for a few seconds so it pours. Measure 15 ml.
4. Pour the gin, lemon juice, syrup and egg white into a shaker. Close it and shake hard with no ice for about 10 seconds, so the white turns to froth.
5. Open it, fill it with ice, and shake hard again for 12 to 15 seconds, until the outside is too cold to hold comfortably.
6. Strain it into the cold coupe through a small tea strainer held over the glass, so the froth comes out smooth.

**closingLine:** *Froth it before the ice goes in. Then tell one joke tonight that's for nobody's good.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A club that teased politicians over dinner had a drink of its own. It was pink.*

**whoYouAre**
Someone at the table has started to believe their own story. A boss, an old friend who's done well, the relative everyone humours. You don't correct them. Correcting them would cost them something with everyone watching. So you make it funny, carefully, aimed at them and not at the room, and they're the one laughing hardest. Nothing else happens that night. A week later, quietly, they've dropped it. Nobody mentions the joke, least of all you.

It sounded like a quip. It took you most of the evening. Nobody guesses how much the untrue thing bothered you while you were smiling: you can sit with almost anything except a story everyone has agreed to believe. The room that frightens you is the one where nobody's allowed to laugh, because that's where it stays true for good. And there's a cost you rarely mention. When you mean something about your own life, people are still waiting for the funny part.

You let people be wrong and keep their dignity. It's kinder than honesty on its own, and much harder.

**yours**

1. In Philadelphia in the 1880s, some journalists started a dining club, the Clover Club. Once a month they had dinner at a hotel there, and they had set out to enjoy good food, plenty of drink and teasing politicians.

2. Politicians were at the table. They'd been invited: in its first two years the club's guests included two former governors and an attorney-general. The guests were toasted from a silver loving cup, then drank from it standing while the members stayed seated. Then came the speeches, and what the club's own book called a "war of wit". The book claims it was kindly meant and well received. And after a few meetings, the club got a baby's chair and a rattle for welcoming each new member.

3. I recognise you in that. They didn't shout from outside. They asked the powerful to dinner, honoured them first, and they'd already made themselves look ridiculous with a rattle. I like to think that's why a guest could laugh along: nobody at that table had to lose face to hear it. You do the same. You go first as the silly one, so the person it's about can take it home.

4. The club had its own cocktail: gin, lemon, raspberry syrup and egg white. Its recipe first turns up in 1901, when the Waldorf-Astoria's head bartender gave it to a paper, the *New York Press*. In 1934 *Esquire* named it one of the ten worst cocktails, and it was all but forgotten until a new bar named itself after it, late in the 2000s, and poured it as its own. It's a classic again, and the cocktail I've made for you is a Clover Club, with a syrup of my own: I make the raspberry syrup with red wine instead of water, as a nod to those dinners, where the wit came with the wine. It looks like the least serious thing you could order, pink under a soft cap of froth. Underneath is a full measure of gin, and the raspberry tastes deeper, of fruit and wine rather than sweets. You only find that out by tasting it. I like to think your best jokes work the same way.

5. Keep telling the truth like that. The people who've been wrong around you are luckier than they know. But every joke of yours is working for something: the truth, the face, whoever it's about. Now and then, make one that carries nothing at all, daft from start to finish, just because it makes you laugh. That club kept a baby's rattle, after all.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Nothing in this glass is pretending. You'd know if it were.*

**whoYouAre**
You're a scientist of the senses. You notice what other people miss: the second flavour hiding behind the first, the moment a drink changes in the glass. And you've taught yourself to put it into words.

Among your friends, you're the one people ask before they choose: the restaurant, the song, the gift, the place to go. It isn't because yours is the loudest opinion. It's because you can always say *why*. That's your gift. You don't just know that something is good, you know what makes it so. It's also how you love people. When you find something wonderful you can't keep it to yourself, and nothing makes you happier than watching someone discover it through you. What you can't forgive is being fooled: the label that promises too much, the story told only to impress.

**yours** (authored base; the live tailoring keeps these paragraphs, anchors and order)

1. You may know a story about this drink's ancestor, the Rob Roy. It's usually told with a grand New York hotel in it. The hotel did serve it, but only once the drink was already a couple of years old. The truer story is more specific and more niche. In the 1890s a salesman walked into a working bar by the Hoboken ferry with a new scotch and asked for a cocktail made with it. Nobody mixed scotch back then. The bartender could have said no. Instead he listened, and invented something on the spot, so that a stranger's whisky could be understood.
2. That story nearly didn't survive. An earlier Rob Roy, twenty years before, was lost when a newspaper printed its recipe wrong. This one lasted because the bartender's brother took the trouble, nearly fifty years later, to write down what really happened. That's you, isn't it? You're the one who takes the trouble. You'd rather have the true story than the famous one, because for you, getting it right is a way of caring.
3. So I made it the way it would resonate with you: the purest truth, with no frills for show. It's stirred rather than shaken, so it stays perfectly clear and you can see all the way through it. There are two sherries in it: a dry one that smells of walnuts, though there isn't a nut in the glass, and a very sweet one that tastes of raisins. They don't blur together. You'll be able to tell them apart, and for someone like you, that's the pleasure. The dry sherry is aged in rows of barrels where the oldest is never completely emptied, so every glass keeps a little of what came before. And a single sage leaf, because sage goes surprisingly well with orange and honey.
4. Here's what I'd ask of you. When you do have this in front of you, take the first sip without naming anything. No notes, no verdict. Name it all on the second, if you still want to. Then try the same thing the next time anything delights you: a meal, a song, a person. Let the first moment go unexplained. You've spent years making sure pleasure tells you the truth. It will. You can put the notebook down.

## Reading

**epigraph**
*Two countries, two whiskies, both often called rye. One usually holds only a little rye.*

**whoYouAre**
You've seen how something could work better: the way the team runs its week, how the family shares out the holidays, the fix a friend has needed for years. You can see it whole. And before you say a word, you walk back through it, more than once, until you can explain it in a sentence. From outside it looks like confidence. It's closer to care. You know that if they like it, they'll actually do it.

What keeps you up is the yes: everyone's, and then finding out you were wrong. A mistake you make alone stays with you. A mistake people take up because of you travels with every one of them.

So you never hand anyone an answer to obey. You give them a way of seeing it, plain enough to use without you, and to notice if you've slipped. You never asked anyone to believe you. You showed them how to look. That's generosity, and not the usual kind: people leave you more capable, not more in need of you.

**yours**

1. In 1977 an English journalist called Michael Jackson (no relation to the singer) published a guide to the world's beer. He'd started at sixteen, writing about pubs for weekly papers in West Yorkshire. His book took beer thoroughly and seriously, and it brought in an idea: beer "styles". Pale ale, porter, pilsner, bock, India pale ale: groups of beers, and how each one relates to the others.

2. Ten years later he did the same for whisky, with a book that showed how the world's whisky types are related. Before then, apart from a handful of earlier books, publishers hadn't imagined anyone would want to read more about whisky than a label. His influence reached writers, readers and drinkers, and brewers and distillers too, many of whom counted him an inspiration, or simply a friend. Perhaps the best tribute to him is that his kind of book, new in its day, now seems obvious.

3. Did it ever keep him up at night? I can't say. But I like to think it did, and that it's why his big idea was a way of grouping, not a verdict: with a style in your head, you can place a beer you've never tasted, by yourself. I see you in that. You don't want people simply following you. You want them to see what you saw, and carry on from there without you.

4. So the cocktail I've made for you is a renowned whiskey classic, an Old-Fashioned, with its whisky drawn from two countries. Canadians often call their whisky "rye", a name from the days when it was wheat whisky flavoured with rye; today most of it is made mainly from corn, usually with a little rye for flavour. American rye whiskey must be at least half rye. Same name, the grains usually swapped, side by side in one glass. To honour his guide to how whiskies relate, I used a guide of my own, a chart of which flavours go together, and looked for a flavour that goes with both grains. I found tamarind, dark and sour, and it gives the drink the sourness it needs to balance. Stirred with ice in a jar, it's strained into a frozen glass with none, and finished with oil pressed from orange peel.

5. You keep the next idea back until you're sure, and you'll never feel quite sure enough. But look at what you've already done to it: you've made it simple enough to see through. People who take up an idea like that aren't following blindly. So share it before it's big. A flaw found among a few friends costs a laugh. And if there's no flaw, you get what you were after all along: people doing something better, their own way, because of what you showed them.

He became a merchant and wine shipper, and over the years he came to believe the trade was being badly run: port mishandled in the making, and the Douro Wine Company, which held a monopoly dating from 1756, taxed exports heavily and limited how much could be shipped. He blamed both for the slump the port trade was in. 2. In 1844 he set it out in a pamphlet, without his name on it. It ran through eight printings fast, so plenty of people wanted a copy. He was easily found out anyway, and bitterly attacked by those with a stake in the trade as it was. I like to think he'd hoped the pages would be judged on their own. 3. What he did next is why I thought of you. He didn't go quiet. By the next year he had more on the same subject in print. And in 1852 he gave evidence to a committee of the House of Commons, under his own name this time, setting out at greater length every abuse his pamphlet had summed up. He wasn't on his own: the people of the wine country backed him warmly. He had a stake too: he shipped port himself, and what that committee was weighing was Britain's duty on wine. And not everyone since agrees he was right about all of it. But what stays with me is the order of things. First the attack, then more of the argument, not less. Most people only ever see the first time you say something. They don't see you checking it again, and coming back with more. 4. So the cocktail I've made for you is port, twice. It's stirred and served like a Martini, with port where the gin would be: first a short measure of young ruby, fresh and fruity, then twice as much tawny, a blend of wines from several years. The same kind of wine, said again at greater length, as a nod to the way he kept saying it. Port tends to be sweet, and rather than add anything to make it go down easier, I dried it with strong, cold black tea. On the flavour chart I work from, port and tea sit in the same family of aromas. Orange oil goes on top, and it's served with no ice, in a small, chilled port glass. 5. When a room goes cold on you, it's tempting to read it as an answer. On bad nights it feels like proof you're wrong. On good ones, like proof you're right. It's neither. Forrester was attacked by the people with a stake and backed by the people of the wine country, and neither of those settled whether he was right. So the next time it goes quiet, let it, and go back to what you found. If it's still there, say it again, with more of it. And if one day it isn't, you'll be the one who says so, out loud. ## Reading

**epigraph**
*Built for a tequila that had to find a name twice. Stone still crushes its agave.*

**whoYouAre**
Two hours into the evening, the table is arguing about something that sounds important: who said what, whose fault it was, what to call it. You've let all of it go. It isn't that you can't follow it. You followed it once, a while back, and found out how little of it was worth the heat. But buried in all that noise there's one small thing nobody else noticed was the point, and that one you won't let go.

Your ease took effort, though nobody sees it. You've been pulled into someone else's story before, and found yourself carrying part of something that wasn't true. So now you step back early. And because you step back, people sometimes decide you don't care. You do. You care about very few things, and you care about those all the way.

That gives people something, and they rarely say it: with you, nobody has to win. The temperature drops. When someone wants an argument to go quiet, they bring it to you.

**yours**

1. Sauza was founded in 1873, and the name grew into one of the biggest in tequila. Then the business was sold, and the name passed from one company to the next: a Spanish firm, then Allied Domecq, Fortune Brands, Beam and Suntory. Today its agave goes through a diffuser, a big industrial machine that breaks it down with steam and chemicals. It came in when agave ran short, and it gets more out of every plant.

2. One piece stayed in the family. As Guillermo Erickson Sauza, the founder's great-great-grandson, tells it, his grandfather kept the family estate in the town of Tequila, and on it an old distillery he'd turned into a museum. Guillermo felt the tequilas he could buy had lost something next to the ones he'd drunk with his grandfather, and he thought getting the old place running again would be a fun project. He wasn't allowed to put the family name on it. He called it Los Abuelos, for the grandfathers before him, and then a rum's trademark forced him to change that too. The name it ended up with was Fortaleza. The old distillery had been called La Fortaleza. Maybe one led to the other. I like to think so.

3. A name is what everyone fights over. Guillermo lost two, and kept the old way going. Over twenty years later, they still cook the agave slowly in a brick oven and crush it with a tahona, a big stone wheel pulled round and round a stone bed, which he'll tell you is far less efficient than a modern mill. As he puts it, they won't make the most tequila, or earn the most from it. I like to think the name was never the part he cared about most.

4. You'd have understood Guillermo straight away. Everyone else was busy with the name: who owned it, who could use it, what to put on the bottle instead. What mattered to him was smaller than all that: a piece of land, an old stone wheel, and a taste he remembered from drinking with his grandfather. You know that kind of small.

5. So the cocktail I've made for you is the simplest long drink there is, and one of the best: Fortaleza Blanco, or another blanco made with a stone wheel, with cold soda and nothing else poured in. No lime, no sugar, nothing covering it up. With soda, a blanco tequila turns bright and citrusy all by itself. The one extra is a sprig of oregano, pinched once and laid on the ice, as a nod to the small thing nobody thought to pick. It shares a note with the tequila, so it brings out something already there.

6. Your way has one cost, though. Because you let so much go, people take your ease for not caring. Next time the table's arguing and the thing you care about is caught in the middle of it, don't just keep hold of it quietly. Tell them, out loud, that it matters to you. The people who thought you were easy about everything will be surprised. Then they'll trust your ease even more, because they'll know it was always your choice.

# Pour — Note to Self · The Scientist (sage-ruler)

## Cocktail

- **name:** Note to Self
- **tagline:** Impressive is easy. Exact is what you're after.
- **glassware:** tall highball glass (about 300 ml), chilled in the freezer, 1-inch ice cubes added one at a time
- **contains:** `[]`

**recipe**

| amount | item | note |
|---|---|---|
| 50 ml | unpeated Highland single malt Scotch whisky | ideally one whose label says it was aged in bourbon casks, with no sherry or wine finish |
| ⅛ teaspoon | pure vanilla extract | the real thing, not "vanilla flavouring"; oak casks give whisky some of the same flavour |
| 100 ml | soda water or seltzer, very cold | straight from the fridge; two parts soda to one of whisky |

**method**
1. Put the glass in the freezer for at least 15 minutes, and the soda in the fridge.
2. Pour the whisky and the vanilla into the cold glass.
3. Lower one ice cube in with a bar spoon so it doesn't crack, and wait about 10 seconds.
4. Stir slowly until drops form on the outside of the glass, about 10 seconds.
5. Add one or two more cubes, until the ice is two-thirds of the way up, and stir briefly.
6. Pour in just enough soda that the ice doesn't float. Push the spoon to the bottom, raise the lowest cube about an inch, and lower it again: that mixes it without knocking out the bubbles.
7. Add a last cube and the rest of the soda. Stir once, a single turn, and serve straight away.

**closingLine:** *Ease the first cube in slowly. Then leave the hunch in the margin, where someone will find it.*

## Reading

**epigraph**
*A careful 1887 book on whisky hardly mentions casks. The vanilla here is for them.*

**whoYouAre**
You know when the boiler was last serviced, what the meter read in March, and how long bread really takes in your oven, not what the packet says. When an argument starts about how things used to be, you don't join in. You fetch the notes.

Some people mistake that for coolness. It isn't. Writing it down is how you keep a messy world still enough to think in. And, though you rarely admit it, it's one of the things you enjoy most. You're better company than your notebook suggests.

What haunts you is the thing you never thought to write down, the one that mattered after all, in a column you didn't make. But when someone needs to know what really changed, nobody has to guess. They count from your numbers, and the count holds.

**yours**

1. In 1885 a London trade paper sent a journalist called Alfred Barnard to visit every whisky distillery in Britain and Ireland. Two years later his reports came out as one book, *The Whisky Distilleries of the United Kingdom*. He's regarded as the first whisky writer. He set down the small details of much of the equipment at each distillery, and a modern reference book on spirits calls his book the earliest and most accurate account of the industry in its day.

2. Writers still count from his numbers. In 1887 he found eighteen distilleries working in what is now the Republic of Ireland. By the 1960s there were three, and that fall is still measured from his eighteen. Old pictures of still houses are captioned as he found them. And yet his book hardly mentions the casks. We don't know why. For all his fussing over detail, he was sociable and funny, and he dotted his reports with scenes from the journey, so the book reads as a travel story too. A hundred years on, it was reprinted.

3. I like to think two things kept it on the shelf: everything he did write down can be checked, and you can tell he was enjoying himself. I see you in both. Your notes will have a gap somewhere. Everyone's do. His gap hasn't stopped people counting from his book.

4. So the cocktail I've made for you is a true classic, the whisky highball: whisky and soda, which took over from brandy and soda in Britain in the second half of the nineteenth century. It's an unpeated Highland single malt, ideally one whose label says it was aged in bourbon casks, lengthened with two parts very cold soda. It's built step by step, and every step has a reason. A frozen glass and cold soda keep the bubbles. The first cube is lowered in slowly, so it doesn't crack. The bottom cube is lifted once, to mix it without knocking out the fizz. I've added one touch: a little real vanilla, as a nod to the casks his book hardly mentions, since oak casks give whisky some of that same flavour. It's there in the recipe, like everything else.

5. Keep the readings, the dates and the bread times exactly as you do. But put yourself in the notes too: the joke, the hunch, the part you loved. The numbers are what people will check. You are what they'll want to read.
